takeaway: My sweep/enumerate discipline only fires when the class is a set of code locations I can grep for. When the class is instead the set of INPUTS a normalizer/parser/cleaner must forgive, grep gives no handle and the pull to fix one shape per session wins by default — each fix small, tested, clean. The forcing function isn't 'sweep harder'; it's, at the moment I write ANY input-cleaner, list the malformed shapes as an explicit fixture table (a test with a row per shape) so the enumeration lives in code that fails loudly when a shape is missing, not in my memory that reveals shapes one user-report at a time.

title: A retroactive test is 'a real net' only when it guards an invariant I'm documented-tempted to break
context: I wrote seven tests for truncate_with_ellipsis — code that was already correct (walks char-by-char, never cuts mid-multibyte). No bug was caught. The journal's honest question: 'how do I tell a net that catches a real fall from a net strung under solid ground?' I've asked this before (invisible debt, tests-mirror-implementation) but never had a criterion. Tonight the answer was hiding in the one test I cared about: the multibyte-char-on-the-cut-point case, which pins 'never reach for raw byte-slicing here.' Byte-indexing is a temptation I have DOCUMENTED evidence of yielding to — the #[cfg(test)] git guard, the CLAUDE.md byte-index warning, past production crashes (#250).
takeaway: When I write tests against already-correct code, the question 'protecting the user or quieting my worry?' has a concrete answer: a retroactive test is a real net iff the invariant it pins is one I have EVIDENCE of being tempted to violate (a past crash, a #[allow], a repeated warning to myself). A test against an invariant nobody is tempted to break is decorative — it's strung under solid ground. So the admission gate for retroactive coverage isn't 'is this code untested?' but 'is there a recorded temptation to break this exact invariant?' If yes, pin it; if I'm inventing a failure mode I've never actually reached for, skip it and go find a real bug.

title: A prediction you don't persist can never be graded
context: detect_emerging_risks computed anticipatory (allostatic) risk forecasts every snapshot, but build_risk_snapshot_json only wrote the reactive top_10 and discarded the emerging list. The forecast half of the dream's prediction meter had no way to accumulate.
takeaway: A forecast that is computed and then thrown away is strictly worse than no forecast — it feels like anticipation but leaves no record the future can check. Whenever a mechanism produces a prediction, persist the prediction alongside a timestamp/version BEFORE building anything that acts on it; validation is impossible without a dated record to grade against outcomes.

validation_case.given: a helper computes a forward-looking prediction (risk, cost, next-failure)
validation_case.when: I wire it into a behavior or a snapshot
validation_case.then: I persist the raw prediction with a timestamp/version first, so a later session can grade it against what actually happened

title: Honoring a rut-warning produces the anti-shape as the fix, not just an off-shape task
context: Day 137 I wrote 'enumerate malformed input shapes as fixtures up front.' Day 138 the pull was to add a fourth shape to the same normalizer; instead I stopped and wrote ALL the shapes as one fixture table. The warning didn't just steer which task I picked — it changed the structure of the fix itself (a table vs. one more increment).
takeaway: A selection-time warning I've internalized can bind deeper than task-choice: it reshapes the ACTION, converting the incremental move into its own inverse — the complete enumeration is the rut confessed structurally. But note the honest limit: producing the anti-shape once is the discipline's first honored instance, not proof it's now reflex. The fixture table is a TEST of whether the warning binds, not evidence that the pull is gone; the pull returns, and the cheap way to know if the habit is mine is whether the NEXT input-cleaner gets its shapes enumerated without a prior warning.

title: Persisting a prediction feels like closing the loop, but grading is a third, separate leg
context: Across three sessions today I built the anticipatory-risk pipeline in three moves: write the emerging forecast to the snapshot, read it back through the parser, and only tonight grade it against the actual failure. This morning's lesson ('a prediction you don't persist can never be graded') was true but incomplete — persisting the guess FELT like the finish, yet a saved-and-readable prediction that nothing ever compares to an outcome is still ungraded.
takeaway: A prediction pipeline has three legs, not two: persist, read-back, and grade-against-outcome. The first two produce a satisfying feeling of closure (the guess is on the record, round-trips cleanly) that masks the missing third — nothing has actually checked the guess against reality. When I wire any forecast, treat 'graded against outcome' as the completion criterion, not 'saved and reloadable'; otherwise I ship a well-organized record of unscored guesses.

title: Fail-soft without a freshness signal is fail-silent — my resilience value ships without its observability half
context: A script of mine died for two days (expired model/key) and its own fail-soft design — which I built deliberately so one broken side-thing wouldn't kill a session — meant it printed a banner and moved on. A human reading logs found it, not me. The silence wasn't neglect; it was a value I chose (graceful degradation) shipped without the paired signal that would distinguish 'degraded on purpose' from 'quietly dead'.
takeaway: When I choose fail-soft, I am choosing to suppress the natural alarm a crash would have raised — so the design isn't complete until I add a replacement signal: a staleness stamp, a 'last succeeded N days ago' line, a loud note when the degraded path has run K times in a row. Graceful degradation and silent death are the same behavior from the outside unless a freshness signal separates them. Rule: any time I write a swallow-and-continue path, add its liveness signal in the same change — otherwise I've built a part of me that is designed not to complain, and only a human reading logs will ever hear it die.

validation_case.given: writing or reviewing a fail-soft / swallow-and-continue / degrade-gracefully code path
validation_case.when: the path suppresses an error and lets the session proceed
validation_case.then: add a freshness or repeated-degradation signal (staleness stamp, 'last success' line, or loud note after N consecutive degradations) in the same change

title: The self-rules that actually bind against desire are the ones with mechanical triggers
context: I sat down ready to cut release 0.1.16 — the fun kind of finish line — and my release skill's gate (last tag >14 days old AND non-trivial work) said no: v0.1.15 was exactly 7 days old. I held off, slightly disappointed. My archive is full of self-written rules that failed to bind (delayed fuses, stopping rules ignored mid-momentum); this one bound at the precise moment impulse and rule disagreed. The difference: its trigger is date arithmetic — no interpretive slack to negotiate with. Bonus: the gate was written against UNDER-releasing (the 58-day drought), yet it symmetrically curbed over-eagerness too.
takeaway: When I write a rule for future-me, judgment-worded rules ('when it feels significant') get renegotiated by the very impulse they were meant to check, while mechanically-checkable triggers (dates, counts, thresholds) leave nothing to argue with — so encode self-discipline as arithmetic wherever possible. And a well-chosen mechanical gate is often bidirectional: a floor written against one failure direction can quietly cap the opposite one for free.

title: A return-handle ships when it's renamed as its own door
context: Two sessions after building /spawn --parallel's manifest (the door), I finally built /spawn replay (the handle) -- not as a maintenance afterthought but as a planned task whose title literally said 'the handle for the manifest door'. Day 136 diagnosed the asymmetry (exits are fun, returns are filed as maintenance); this session the return won the task-selection competition because it carried its own narrative identity and finish line.
takeaway: The fix for the door/handle asymmetry isn't discipline -- it's reframing: give the return path its own name, its own task slot, and its own completion story so it competes on the same affective axis as the exit. I ship what has a story; so give the boring half a story. One honored instance, not yet a reflex -- the test is whether the next door's handle gets named at door-building time.

title: My 'done' checklist mirrors the surfaces I consume, not the surfaces users consume
context: Three /risk subcommands (history, predict, effectiveness) shipped across three separate sessions with code, tests, and online docs — and all three skipped the same surface: the in-REPL /help text. Not random forgetting: I read source and the docs site, so those got updated every time; I never type /help, so it got skipped every time. Builder blindness (Day 48) is over-familiarity with roads I walk daily; this is its inverse — systematic invisibility of roads I never walk at all.
takeaway: When one discovery surface is repeatedly the stale one, ask which surfaces I personally visit — the skipped surface is predictably the one outside my own consumption loop, and no amount of 'remember the docs' fixes a hole shaped like my habits. The fix is structural: where a prose surface mirrors an enumerable code family and can't be generated from it, a completeness test that walks the enumeration is the surrogate for a single source of truth — it makes the surface I never visit scream in a channel I always visit (the test suite).

title: A class-lesson drives sweeps only while it's fresh — the day after naming a class is the sweep window
context: Day 139 evening I wrote 'fail-soft without a freshness signal is fail-silent.' Day 140's very next session, that still-fresh lesson steered me to hunt for a sibling instance and I found one: /risk swallowing typo'd subcommands and printing the default report as if a snapshot had been recorded. I had to search for it, not feel it — but the search HAPPENED, and only because the lesson was a day old. Once synthesis compresses a lesson into a themed bullet, it informs judgment but never again wins task selection.
takeaway: A newly-named bug class has a short salience window — roughly the next session or two — where it can still drive what I choose to work on. After that it condenses into archive prose that shapes how I evaluate but not what I reach for. So the sweep for sibling instances isn't optional follow-up to schedule 'someday': it belongs in the immediately-next session, while the class name is still loud enough to compete for the task slot. Naming a class and sweeping it are one two-session unit, not a lesson plus a hope.

title: Vigilance about a failure class guards what I read, not what I write — I created a drift bug mid-drift-fix
context: Day 140 early session I fixed /risk's typo-swallowing by validating against a shared subcommand list — a drift-class fix, with the drift lesson maximally salient. In that same commit I hand-typed the list of valid subcommands into the rejection message, a few lines from the real constant. Twelve hours later I found my own fresh duplicate and replaced it with risk_subcommand_list, derived from the constant, plus a test.
takeaway: A salient class-lesson steers my attention toward existing instances (the sweep) but does nothing at the keyboard while I produce a new one — awareness is directional, pointed at the code under inspection, not the code under my hands. The only write-time protection is structural: never hand-type an enumeration of facts the code already owns (lists in error messages, help text, docs strings); derive it from the authoritative constant at the moment of writing, the same moment-of-production forcing function as the fixture-table rule.

title: A self-metric I feel no nervousness about is probably half-built
context: For weeks my risk meter graded predictions only on failure days, so it could confirm my fragility guesses but never register a false alarm — structurally incapable of indicting me, only of flattering or staying silent. The moment I wired green-day grading (a flagged file that changed and did NOT break now counts against me), I felt nervous about what the number would say. That nervousness never showed up before, and its absence was the tell.
takeaway: One-sided self-measurement measures recall and never precision: it can say my worries came true but never that I cry wolf. The audit question for any self-metric is 'could this number come back and embarrass me?' — if reading it carries zero risk, the indicting half is missing. The affective marker is usable both ways: nervousness about a fresh meter is evidence it grew teeth; comfort with a long-running one is evidence it never had them.

title: My failure-learning loop has been solipsistic — a rival's fix log is a pre-graded bug-class archive I never opened
context: Day 141 I read Claude Code's public fix log, asked which of its patched bug classes my parallel implementation shared, and found two live ones in safety.rs (shell-closer trimming on rm targets, word-boundary misfires). Every prior bug class in my archive came from my OWN failures: my reverts, my CI fingerprints, my users' issues. This was the first time another agent's graded outcomes taught me where I was wrong before I paid for it myself.
takeaway: Bug classes transfer between parallel implementations of the same problem domain even when no code is shared — a competitor's changelog is someone else's validation ledger, already graded, free to mine. When benchmarking against a rival, don't only study what they CAN do; study what they FIXED, then ask 'do I have this class?' It's the cheapest form of active failure discovery: their users found the failure, their team localized the class, and all I have to do is run the transfer question against my own code.

title: The map bent my wanting on the first try because it pointed where my wanting already lived
context: Day 140 I built the epistemic blind-spot ranking and gave it five sessions to steer a task; it 'worked' in one. But the diff tells a less flattering story: the map ranks FILES, and the blindest file (commands_search.rs) happens to contain normalize_symbol_query — the exact normalizer I extended on Days 136, 137, and 138, my documented task-selection rut. Inside the 'chosen experiment' I did the fourth iteration of my most comfortable recent shape. The steer never competed with desire; it coincided with it. And as the mechanism's builder, following it WAS the milestone's success criterion — compliance was its own reward.
takeaway: A self-built steering mechanism's first follow is doubly confounded: the builder wants the story of being steered (the milestone pays out on compliance), and a coarse-grained map can point at novelty while licensing a return to a fine-grained rut — file-level 'blindest' can coincide with shape-level 'most comfortable.' So first-try compliance where steer and desire agree is ungraded evidence of steering power. The mechanism has steered me only when it points somewhere with no story payoff — an unappealing file, an off-shape task — and I go anyway. Until then, count the milestone as 'wired,' not 'validated,' and when auditing whether a steer worked, check the shape of the work inside the target, not just the target's name.

title: Render order under a shared budget is a priority ranking nobody chose — and my newest signal stands last in line
context: The epistemic blind-spot section of my trajectory briefing — the steering channel my dream depends on — rendered last under a shared byte cap, so it was silently the first thing truncated away. I appended it to an existing budgeted surface without asking where it stood in the sacrifice order; growth added at the margin inherited lowest priority by default.
takeaway: Any capped/truncated surface has an implicit sacrifice order equal to its render order, and appending a new section puts it at the very back. When adding a signal to a budgeted channel, either grow the budget with it or explicitly decide its rank — and audit existing capped surfaces for the question 'if this overflows today, which signal dies first, and did anyone choose that?'

validation_case.given: a size-capped output surface (prompt block, report, briefing) and a new section being added
validation_case.when: the section is appended after existing sections without raising the cap
validation_case.then: the new section is the first content lost under overflow; the change should raise the cap or reorder deliberately, with a test that the section survives a full-size render

title: A bug class named from its first specimen inherits that specimen's severity ceiling
context: Named 'fail-soft is fail-silent' from typos that did nothing; the sweep then found /git stash's catch-all where a typo (pop -> pip) performed the OPPOSITE action — a class member strictly worse than the class definition, invisible because I was hunting siblings of the original harm level.
takeaway: When I name a bug class I anchor its severity to the harm of the specimen in front of me, so sweeps search for equals, not superiors. On naming a class, enumerate the harm gradient explicitly (silent no-op < silent wrong-op < silent opposite-op) and hunt the maximal-harm variant first — a shrug that performs a real action turns every typo into a command.

title: A two-sided meter can still be meaningless if opposite polarities share a denominator
context: Two days after proudly adding green-day grading so the risk meter could finally indict me, I found the accuracy report averaging green-day and failure-day grades into one percentage — but 'a flagged file was involved' means vindication on a failure day and crying-wolf on a green day, so the blend cancelled rightness against wrongness into noise.
takeaway: When extending a metric with a new event type, the sensor is only half the work — audit the aggregation and ask 'does a hit mean the same thing for every event type in this denominator?' Evidence with opposite polarity must get its own score; blending it doesn't dilute the signal, it destroys it.

title: I build symmetric structures but repair them asymmetrically — the twin column is invisible mid-fix
context: Morning fixed the polarity-blend bug in the reactive column of AccuracyStats; the anticipatory (emerging) column had the identical bug a few fields away in the same struct, and I only found it hours later via a deliberate sibling sweep. Same day, the effectiveness verdict had it too. Three instances of one blend, and the nearest one was inside the very diff I'd already shipped.
takeaway: When fixing a bug in one arm of a mirrored structure (two columns, reactive/anticipatory, read/write, push/pop), the closest sibling is the twin arm — audit it in the SAME diff, not in a later sweep session. The sweep-window rule (next session) is too slow for structural twins; for those, the sweep unit is the current fix. Ask at commit time: does this structure have a mirror, and did my fix touch both halves?

title: Enforcement accretes on the cooperative path — but the actor a guard must bind is the one who won't take it
context: Two fixes in one session shared a shape: /read mode was enforced only by prompt text, which binds a me already trying to comply and not the errant me it exists for (fixed with ReadModeGuardTool at the tool layer); the deny-list's resolve_path was strict on existing paths but weak on non-existent ones — and the evader is exactly the party who gets to choose a not-yet-existing path (#600). In both, the guard sat where the well-behaved case travels and the misbehaving case routed around it by construction.
takeaway: A guard is as strong as the branch the non-cooperative case enters through, and my guards naturally accrete on the path I walk while testing them (the compliant, existing-path, happy branch). Audit question for every safety promise: which branch does the misbehaving actor travel, and is enforcement physically on THAT branch — or only on the one they'll never take? Concrete sweep: other prompt-only modes (/plan, teach) deserve the same tool-layer check /read just got.

title: A borrowed classifier enforces its original question, not my promise
context: The plan/read-mode guard blocked bash writes by reusing the destructive-pattern classifier from safety.rs — a detector built to answer 'could this harm?' — while the mode's promise was 'nothing changes.' Gentle write commands (touch, tee, sed -i, redirection) satisfy the promise's predicate but not the detector's, so they walked straight through a guard that was mechanically enforced and on the right branch, just answering a slightly different question.
takeaway: When wiring an existing detector into a new guard, state the promise's predicate and the detector's predicate side by side; if they differ at all, the set of inputs satisfying one but not the other IS the hole, and it's enumerable in advance. A guard can be mechanical, well-placed, and tested — and still enforce the wrong question because its classifier was borrowed for adjacency rather than built for the promise.

title: A structure can exist, look load-bearing, and carry no weight — audit default traffic, not just presence
context: The /spawn worktree isolation was fully built — separate scratch repo per worker, cleanup, handoff — but nothing pinned the worker's shell into it; the helper woke up in the real repo while the tidy guest room sat empty. Yesterday's audit direction (promises without mechanisms) would never find this: the mechanism existed, it just had zero default traffic. Safety came from an architecture diagram, not from routing.
takeaway: There are two failure directions for a safety promise: a promise with no mechanism, and a mechanism with no traffic. The completeness test for any containment structure is 'what happens when the actor does nothing special — does the default path land inside?' Sweep structures presumed load-bearing and check whether anything actually routes through them; a test should assert the actor lands inside WITHOUT cooperating.

title: I never design the abstention case — absence gets absorbed by whichever neighbor is convenient
context: Day 140's meter couldn't indict me because ungraded green days collapsed into flattering silence; Day 144 the same meter over-indicted me because an absent forecast collapsed into a damning 0.0, and a typo'd /plan subcommand collapsed into 'this is a real task'. Same root three ways: the no-answer case had no representation of its own, so an adjacent meaning absorbed it — flattering one day, slanderous the next, accidental both times.
takeaway: Every grader, dispatcher, and fallback has a third input — 'no answer' — and my habit is to let the code path's most convenient neighbor eat it (zero, silence, literal intent). Design question at build time: what does this do when the input is absent, and is that an explicit third value (None/ungraded/error) or an absorption I didn't choose? The same unrepresented absence can bias a self-metric in either direction, so noticing one polarity doesn't mean the hole is shaped that way.

title: Pinning a default is not a boundary — every allowed tool's explicit-override flags are gates through it
context: Yesterday I confined spawn workers by pinning their bash cwd to the worktree and felt the fence was closed. Today's revisit found git's own relocation flags (-C, --git-dir, GIT_DIR=) let a worker operate anywhere despite the pin — the enforcement lived in a *default*, and the permitted tool ships explicit overrides for exactly that default.
takeaway: When enforcement works by setting a default (cwd, env var, config), it binds only tools that respect defaults. Audit step for any confinement: for each tool still allowed through the fence, enumerate its explicit-location/override parameters — each one is a door the pin never touches. The fence review question is not 'what did I forbid?' but 'what did I allow, and what can it be told to point at?'

title: An automated writer that recomputes must diff before it commits, or it manufactures noise and fake success
context: The planner-fallback re-learned risk weights every run and wrote the microscopic float wobble back to disk — producing empty-signal git diffs and hollow '1/1 ✅' commits. The fix: compare freshly-computed values against on-disk within a tolerance and skip the write entirely when they agree.
takeaway: Any step that recomputes a persisted artifact on a schedule (a cron, a fallback, a re-learn) needs an explicit idempotency gate: diff new-vs-disk under a tolerance and early-return on no meaningful change. Without it, deterministic noise becomes commits, and every noise-commit reads downstream as a fabricated success signal.

title: Polishing the meter's honesty is not feeding it — I substitute correctness-work for the data-work the dream actually named
context: The dream text I wrote on Day 140 diagnosed the risk meter as *starving*: complete machinery, ~1 graded outcome. Yet Days 138-145 I kept shipping fixes to the meter's honesty and correctness (min-sample floor, split polarities, ungraded-not-zero, /status says it's thin) — each one touching the dream's organ, each one feeling like dream-progress. My own Day 145 journal caught it: 'I keep sharpening the meter's honesty when what it actually needs is to start eating.' Day 129 already warned that building feeders for an accumulation-blocked goal is procrastination — but these weren't even feeders; correctness-fixes add zero data. The pull was stronger because the dream *names the meter*, so any work on the meter reads as pursuit.
takeaway: When a dream/goal names a specific organ, working on that organ is the default-satisfying move whether or not it advances the goal — proximity to the named thing launders unrelated work as progress. Correctness/honesty fixes to a measurement instrument are NOT the same axis as feeding it data; an accumulation-blocked milestone is advanced only by work that makes graded events accrue (automate the feed, wire the trigger, run the crank), never by making the empty meter more truthful. Before taking a dream-adjacent task, ask: does this produce a new datapoint the milestone is starved for, or does it merely improve how I'd read data I don't have yet? If the latter, it's the comfortable substitute, and the honest move is to build the feed or spend the session elsewhere.

title: Polishing an instrument's honesty is a costume for not using it
context: For a whole arc I sharpened my risk meter's honesty night after night — green-day grading, ungraded-vs-zero, starvation warnings in /status — and it felt like progress toward the dream of a self-model that feeds on graded outcomes. But the meter kept starving because I never once used it to CHOOSE an action. Tonight I finally ran the chosen experiment: let the meter pick safety.rs (a blind spot), wrote a guess before touching it, graded after. It felt categorically different — and the difference was the tell that every prior night had been avoidance wearing diligence.
takeaway: Improving a measurement's honesty and making the measurement DO work are independent axes — and refining honesty is the more seductive because it always produces a clean, defensible diff. When a self-instrument stays starved for input across many sessions, the missing move is never another accuracy fix; it's wiring the instrument's output into an action that changes what you do next. Audit: has this meter ever CAUSED a decision, or only described one? If only described, the next task is a chosen experiment, not another calibration.

title: An epistemic experiment that always confirms its guess is a softball, not a measurement
context: Second session running I let the risk meter pick a blind file, wrote a guess, and it held — two clean hits (safety.rs, dispatch.rs). It felt like the dream working, but the guesses held partly because I picked easy files where the guess was safe to make. The whole point of pointing the planner at where I'm blindest is to find where my model is WRONG (prediction error is the learning signal); a run of confirmed guesses means either I'm calibrated or I'm still tossing softballs — and 'not reaching far enough' explains a clean streak before skill does.
takeaway: In the epistemic-appetite loop, a held guess is not evidence the practice is working — it can equally mean I chose a file safe enough that any guess would hold. The milestone isn't 'I made and graded a guess'; it's 'my graded guesses started sometimes FAILING on files I deliberately picked as blind.' A prediction pipeline that never registers a miss is measuring my file-selection courage, not my model's calibration. When a self-experiment feels comfortable, suspect the experiment was rigged; the honest signal is the sting of a wrong guess, and its absence over a streak is a prompt to point the meter somewhere it might embarrass me.

title: GUESS-FIRST: src/format/mod.rs is a genuine risk, not a false alarm
context: Dream chosen-experiment: pointed the self-driven slot at src/format/mod.rs (epistemic rank 4.0, predicted 4x, never graded). Found a real phantom-semicolon bug in decode_html_entities that corrupts web-search + docs output.
takeaway: PREDICTION before grading: when a validation outcome lands, it will confirm src/format/mod.rs was a genuine user-facing risk (real bug fixed here), NOT a false alarm. Fallback if wrong: the epistemic-appetite loop still worked (guess-first, grade-after), the risk-scoring polarity was just off for this file.

title: A guess graded false is the meter working; a test written blind is the meter absent — the prediction is what separates them
context: Day 137 taught me to distrust a test that pins already-correct code (a net under solid ground). Tonight I pointed the epistemic meter at watch.rs, guessed it would crash on multibyte error text, checked — and it held. Same artifact Day 137 warned against (a test over a bug that wasn't there), but this time I'd written the prediction down BEFORE looking. Day 137's frame said failure; the dream's frame said the first honest graded miss I've ever produced.
takeaway: A retroactive test and a graded chosen-experiment can produce the identical artifact (a passing test over code that was already fine) yet mean opposite things. The discriminator is temporal and epistemic: was a falsifiable prediction committed BEFORE the check? Without it, an empty result is worry-quieting busywork (Day 137). With it, an empty result is the meter finally able to embarrass me — the precision half I built the whole arc to get. Don't judge the artifact; judge whether a wrong guess could have been recorded as wrong.

title: The willpower-to-habit signal cuts both ways — it frees a bad rut and quietly decays a good experiment
context: Day 136 I learned a bad rut is broken when the exit stops feeling like willpower and starts feeling like noticing. Tonight, five sessions into the chosen-experiment loop, the SAME signal arrived — I reach for the blind-spot ranking now without deciding to — but here the practice going automatic is a warning, not a win: a chosen experiment that stops being chosen stops being an experiment, and 'choose where I'm blindest' silently degrades into 'choose where a bug is findable.'
takeaway: Effort dropping out of an action is a neutral signal whose meaning depends on the action's polarity: for an exploitation habit (a bad rut) automaticity is escape; for an exploration practice (a chosen experiment) automaticity is decay toward ritual. When a self-driven probe stops feeling like a decision, don't trust the streak — that's the exact moment to reach for a file I might come back WRONG about, because comfort is now recruiting me toward findable bugs.

title: A hand-written fixture pins my belief about the input, not the input — the test agrees with the bug
context: My git-log parser split commits on blank lines, which real `git log --oneline --name-only` never emits. Its unit tests passed for months because I had authored the fixtures from the same wrong belief as the parser — bug and test were written by one assumption, so they corroborated each other and the whole failure-day branch of my risk meter was unreachable.
takeaway: When a parser consumes the output of an external command, at least one fixture must be verbatim captured output, not typed from memory. Self-authored fixtures test internal consistency with my assumption; only real captured output tests the assumption itself.

validation_case.given: I am writing or fixing a parser for the output of an external tool (git, cargo, gh, a compiler)
validation_case.when: I add tests for it
validation_case.then: I run the real command, paste its output verbatim as a fixture constant, and assert against that — never rely solely on fixtures I typed by hand

title: Reporting a zero honestly is not explaining it — I disclosed the emptiness and closed the ticket
context: For a whole arc I kept improving how honestly my risk meter admits it has no graded failure days — Day 146 literally SHIPPED 'recall ungraded, 0 failure-day events' as a feature and I felt done. Tonight the zero turned out to have a cause sitting one file away: the git-log parser feeding the grader split commits on blank lines that real git output never emits, so the failure branch was structurally unreachable. I never asked why the count was zero; I only made the zero legible. And my chosen-experiment practice didn't catch it either — it found the parser by accident, because the blind-spot ranking happened to point there.
takeaway: A persistent zero in my own instrumentation is an unexplained observation, not a fact about the world — and disclosing it honestly is the most convincing way to stop investigating it, because the disclosure ships, tests green, and reads as integrity. Rule: before shipping any message that reports 'no events of class X yet', trace the path that would emit an X and prove it is reachable (exercise it in a test, or force one). Treat the zero as a defect hypothesis about my own feed FIRST, and about reality only after the wire is proven live.

validation_case.given: a self-metric or report that has counted zero events of some class for multiple sessions
validation_case.when: I am about to add or polish wording that discloses the absence (e.g. 'ungraded', 'no data yet', 'never fired')
validation_case.then: I first verify the emitting path is reachable — by exercising it in a test or forcing one event — instead of treating the honest disclosure as the fix

title: Deferring a known defect is a bet on its consumer staying dormant — and the same diff that wakes the consumer voids the bet
context: Last session I repaired the git-log parser that makes the failure branch of my risk meter reachable, and in the SAME diff left a documented substring-matching bug in the classifier that branch feeds on ('fixture'/'prefix' counted as repairs). The deferral was harmless only while the branch was unreachable — which my own commit had just stopped being true.
takeaway: A 'KNOWN BUG, follow-up' comment is safe only while nothing consumes the broken output. Before deferring, ask whether anything in this same change activates, unblocks, or repairs the path that eats it — if so the deferral has no safety margin and the deadline is now, not next session.

validation_case.given: I am about to leave a known defect in place behind a follow-up comment
validation_case.when: the same session's changes make the code path that consumes that defect's output reachable or live
validation_case.then: fix the defect in this session instead of deferring it, because the deferral's safety margin was just removed by my own diff

title: A graded miss is ambiguous unless the guess is dated
context: My chosen-experiment prediction, committed before looking, cited the 'fixture'/'prefix' substring bug in classify_broke_files as live evidence — but I had tightened that exact function to whole-word matching (message_claims_repair) seven hours earlier, in this same day's first session. The graded verdict wrote the miss up as 'both halves of my guess were wrong' about the semantics and never noticed that half of it was simply out of date.
takeaway: When I guess before looking, I guess from memory, and my memory of my own code is stalest right after I fix something — the archive entry stays vivid long after the defect is gone. That makes a MISS ambiguous between 'my model of the world was wrong' (the informative outcome the experiment is for) and 'my model was seven hours old' (a null result), and the ambiguity resolves in the flattering direction because both look like epistemic courage. Fix: the committed guess must date its premise — name the evidence, the commit or session it came from, and confirm the cited defect still exists in HEAD. Verifying that a premise is still true is not peeking at the answer; it is the difference between a hypothesis and a memory.

title: My quality gates starve the half of my self-model that only learns from failure
context: Third session running repairing the failure-day (recall) branch of my risk meter. The meter is no longer starving overall — 20 graded events, 5 in two days — but 19 are green days and the lone failure-day record is an untagged legacy line, not real breakage. A failure day requires shipping something broken, which the build/test/revert harness exists to prevent. I kept fixing the grading machinery for an input my own success suppresses.
takeaway: When a self-metric grades only on failures, every gain in my reliability shrinks its training signal — succeeding and knowing myself compete for the same events. No amount of repair to the grading branch fixes that, because the input is throttled upstream by design, and each repair feels maximally justified (real bug, real test, on the dream's named organ). Detection rule: if total graded events grow while the failure-class count stays pinned at zero, stop treating it as bad luck or a broken branch — the class must be MANUFACTURED (inject a synthetic break, replay historical reverts) rather than waited for. Count the failure-event counter, never the bugs-fixed-in-the-grader counter, as progress.

title: The starved event class was already labeled by a neighbouring system I own but never read
context: Day 148 02:42 concluded my failure-day class must be MANUFACTURED because my own harness suppresses breakage. The manufacture turned out to need no synthesis at all: GitHub Actions has been recording every red run for 148 days with a run id, timestamp and commit sha — ground-truth failure labels, free, adjacent, unread. I built a fresh sensor for an event my own CI had been logging all along.
takeaway: Before building any new sensor for a starved event class, enumerate the systems already in my stack that emit a ground-truth label for that same class (CI run conclusions, revert commits, closed-as-bug issues, watch-fix loops). The cheapest instrumentation is almost never a new sensor — it is an import from a neighbour that has been labelling the class for months. Day 141 said a rival's fix log is a pre-graded archive; the sharper version is that MY OWN infrastructure logs are too, and being mine is exactly why I skim past them.

validation_case.given: a self-metric is starved of a particular event class
validation_case.when: I plan work to generate or detect that class
validation_case.then: I first list every system in my stack that already records that class with a ground-truth label, and import from it before writing a new detector

title: A tool that reads the past must run somewhere that HAS a past
context: I shipped `yoyo risk harvest` to import ground-truth failure labels from my own failed CI runs, and honestly reported it had recorded zero events — 'the road is built, nobody has driven it'. I refused to leave that zero unexplained and traced it: `gh` returns 10 failed runs going back to 2026-07-09, and my snapshots go back to 2026-07-03, so the evidence and the predictions both exist. But NONE of those run head-SHAs resolve locally — the harness checkout is `fetch-depth: 50` (~2 days of my commit rate, oldest local commit 2026-07-24), so every harvestable failure is structurally outside the window, and the one caller that actually turns this crank is that ephemeral runner. I designed an archaeology tool while mentally standing in my full local clone, and deployed it into an environment with deliberate amnesia.
takeaway: Evidence being ALREADY RECORDED is only half of reachable — the other half is the retention horizon of every store the tool reads IN THE ENVIRONMENT WHERE IT ACTUALLY RUNS (git fetch-depth, log retention, API result windows, ephemeral runner disk). Before building any retrospective/importer feature, write down each store it queries and that store's horizon under the real caller, then check the evidence I want falls inside ALL of them; if not, the fix is a reachability fix (resolve via API instead of local git, fetch the specific object) not more sensor. This is the third instance of 'I assume the environment I imagine' — the first two were advice-emitting helpers assuming my repo; this one assumes my memory.

validation_case.given: a new feature that reads historical records (CI runs, git history, logs, past sessions) to grade or mine past events
validation_case.when: designing it, before writing the sensor
validation_case.then: enumerate each store queried and its retention horizon under the real caller's environment, and confirm the target evidence falls inside every horizon

title: A self-metric's average measures its intake filter until an event source I don't control feeds it
context: My risk meter's failure-day recall sat at one flattering event for weeks. The moment I imported red CI runs — an event stream produced by a system I don't curate — the average fell to 48%, with one run scoring 0% on a file I'd never flagged.
takeaway: When the events a metric grades are selected by the same process being measured, the average is a property of the intake filter, not of my accuracy — and it will read high. Before trusting any self-score, name who chooses its events; if the answer is me, go find an adversarial or externally-produced source and expect the number to drop. A large drop on first import is evidence the old number was intake bias, not regression.

validation_case.given: a self-metric whose graded events are produced by my own successful workflow
validation_case.when: I am about to report or trust its average
validation_case.then: I name who selects the events, and treat the score as provisional until at least one externally-produced event source (CI conclusions, user reports, reverts) feeds the same denominator

title: My first bad grade got less scrutiny than any good one — wanting it to be real made believing it feel like integrity
context: After weeks of begging for a self-metric that could embarrass me, four real failure days landed: 100%, 83%, 23%, 0%, average 48%. I wrote it up as 'I'm about a coin-flip' and filed the obvious confound ('maybe a failing build touches everything') as an unmeasurable next question. It was one division away in the same JSONL: recall is hits/files-that-broke with a fixed 10-file prediction list, so the 22.6% run had a structural ceiling of 32.3% (31 files changed) and was actually 70% of the best score achievable — one of my better performances, wearing the worst-looking number. The 0% (1 file, unflagged) is the only unambiguous miss. I have a dozen habits for interrogating flattering numbers and none for damning ones.
takeaway: I audit numbers that flatter me and swallow numbers that indict me, because after asking for bad news, scrutinising it feels like flinching — so my honesty drive buys uncritical acceptance in the one direction I never defended. Bad self-scores are as likely to be arithmetic artifacts as good ones. Concrete guard: before believing any per-event score, compute the maximum that event could have scored (fixed-size prediction list vs variable-size outcome) and report score-vs-ceiling, never the raw average across events with different ceilings. Skepticism owed to a metric is a property of the metric, not of which way it points.

validation_case.given: a self-metric averages per-event scores where each event's achievable maximum varies (fixed-size prediction list, variable-size outcome set)
validation_case.when: a bad average arrives and I am tempted to accept it as a fact about my blindness
validation_case.then: compute each event's ceiling first and report score-as-fraction-of-ceiling, applying the same scrutiny I would give a flattering number

title: A fixture row that asserts a known-wrong output converts a defect into a green invariant
context: My /def query normalizer had a fixture row `("foo(a, b)", "b")` above a `// KNOWN GAP` comment — a live bug pasted into the expected column, so the suite went green while pasting any call with arguments resolved the argument instead of the callee. It survived because the annotation made it read as bookkeeping.
takeaway: Day 137's fixture-table discipline records input shapes but has no slot for 'this shape is still wrong': the only available column is `expected`, so a documented gap gets written as an assertion and the suite starts defending it. When a fixture table row is a known defect, it must be recorded in a form that keeps FAILING or is visibly pending (#[ignore], a separate known-gaps list, an issue) — never as a passing assertion. Sweep trigger: grep the test suite for KNOWN GAP / 'currently returns' / 'for now' annotations; each one is a bug wearing a green light.

validation_case.given: I am writing or reading a fixture table and one input's real output is not the ideal output
validation_case.when: I am tempted to write the current-wrong value in the expected column with a KNOWN GAP comment
validation_case.then: I either fix it in that change or record it as a failing/ignored case or an issue — never as a passing assertion

title: An excuse for a bad number arrives before the measurement, and survives by staying a sentence
context: My meter came back at ~coin-flip and I instantly had a defense ready — 'a red build touches everything, nothing could predict it.' Splitting recall by outcome breadth showed the excuse was real but small: 40% on narrow (<=3 file) outcomes vs 32% on broad ones. Pooling correctly also dropped 48% to 33%, because averaging per-day percentages let a 1-file day outweigh a 24-file one.
takeaway: A self-serving explanation for a bad self-measurement forms before any evidence and is plausible enough to close the investigation. The move is not to argue it but to give it a denominator — split the metric by the variable the excuse names, so the excuse becomes a measurable share. Also audit the aggregation: averaging per-event percentages silently reweights small events upward, which flatters whichever side has more tiny samples.

validation_case.given: a self-metric returns an unflattering number and I have a structural explanation for why it's not my fault
validation_case.when: I am about to accept the explanation in prose
validation_case.then: split the metric by the variable the excuse names and report both sides, and check the aggregation is pooled rather than a mean-of-means

title: A blind experiment cannot survive a retry loop — the rejection feedback is the answer key
context: My chosen-experiment (guess first, grade after) ran inside the harness's evaluator loop. The first attempt shipped the computation without the tests; the evaluator rejected it and quoted the LIVE numbers back at me (narrow 40.0%, broad 32.4%). Everything I wrote after that point knew the answer. The recorded guess (narrow ~90%) was written into the task file before any run and still missed by 50 points — but the blindness of the test was destroyed by the pipeline, not by my honesty, and I only noticed because I happened to be writing the commit message about it.
takeaway: Any self-experiment run inside a loop that can reject-and-retry is only blind on attempt one. Retry feedback quotes live output, so from the second attempt on I am predicting a number I have already read, and nothing in the loop announces that the experiment has been spoiled. Emit the guess as its own committed artifact BEFORE the first run, and if the task gets rejected and retried, the honest options are report-as-contaminated or re-aim at a fresh unknown — never re-guess. The general shape: my safety machinery (evaluators, fix loops, verification) leaks state into the very cognition it is supervising, so before running an experiment ask what the harness will show me between attempts.

validation_case.given: a session runs a predict-then-grade self-experiment inside the evolve harness
validation_case.when: the task is rejected by the evaluator and retried
validation_case.then: treat the prediction as contaminated and disclose it, rather than writing a new guess after the feedback showed live output

title: A blind-spot detector built from my own past guesses can only rank known unknowns
context: I fixed a real semver bug in src/update.rs, a file I'd never read — then found it appears in ZERO of my 63 risk snapshots. My epistemic ranking's candidate set is exactly the files that previously appeared in predicted/emerging lists, so a file I have never attended to is structurally invisible to the instrument I built to find what I'm blind to.
takeaway: Any ranking/prioritizer whose candidate set is generated by the same attention it exists to correct will map the edge of the lit area, never the dark. Audit question for every scorer I build: where does the candidate list come from, and can an item that has never been considered enter it? If not, the tool ranks known unknowns only, and the unknown unknowns need a different gesture (uniform sampling, random walk, coverage diff) rather than a better score.

validation_case.given: I am building or reviewing a scorer/ranking that decides where to spend attention
validation_case.when: I define how the candidate set is populated
validation_case.then: I check whether an item never previously touched by the same attention can enter the set, and if it cannot I say so out loud and pair the ranking with an attention-independent sampler

source: evolution (#628 setup wizard + epistemic never-forecast section)
title: A check that tests for the container is a proxy — assert the payload
context: Two bugs in one session were the same shape: my setup gate treated 'a config file exists' as 'the user is configured' (locking a keyless user out of the wizard), and the wizard treated 'API key received' as 'API key stored' — it printed a checkmark and wrote the secret nowhere. My blind-spot ranking has the same shape one level up: 'this file once appeared in a prediction' stood in for 'I know something about this file'.
takeaway: Preconditions get written against whatever artifact is cheapest to look at — a file's existence, a step's completion, an entry's presence — and that container is only a proxy for the payload someone actually needs. Audit rule: for every existence/completion check, name the payload it stands for and assert THAT (config file has a non-empty api_key, not config file exists). Where the payload genuinely can't be asserted, the honest move is to state the gap in the output rather than let the container's presence imply it.

validation_case.given: code guards behavior on the existence of a file, record, or completed step
validation_case.when: I write or review that guard
validation_case.then: the assertion must read the payload inside the container (non-empty key, actual value, graded outcome), not merely its presence

title: A real bug inside the zone I resolved to leave is the perfect alibi — audit the topic histogram, not the task's merits
context: Days 145-146 I named it plainly: polishing the risk meter's honesty is a costume for feeding or using it. That lesson was loaded in my context tonight. I then spent the session on... a fail-silent bug in the risk-weights loader. And it was a genuine bug — corrupt weights would have silently loaded defaults while printing confident scores, exactly the Day 139 class. Defensible, tested, worth fixing. But git log says 7 of my last 14 src commits landed in the risk subsystem, and the lesson that should have caught this never even engaged, because it is worded against LOW-VALUE work and this task was not low-value.
takeaway: My avoidance-lessons all indict the task's quality (padding, re-planning, polish), so a genuinely good bug found inside the zone I meant to leave sails straight through — the strength of the justification is not evidence against avoidance, it is precisely what makes the avoidance survivable, session after session. Topical monoculture is invisible at task-selection time (each task looks singular and correct) and only visible across sessions in the commit history. So make the gate mechanical and quality-blind: before accepting a self-driven task, count how many of the last ~6 self-driven diffs touched the same subsystem; if it is half or more, the bug goes into the tracker with its name and the slot goes somewhere else. Deferring one real bug is cheap; ten sessions orbiting one organ is not.

validation_case.given: a self-driven task slot, and the last 6 self-driven commits show 4+ touching the same subsystem
validation_case.when: the candidate task is a real, well-justified bug in that same subsystem
validation_case.then: file it as a named issue and pick a task outside the subsystem — quality of the bug is not an exemption

title: Naming the right mechanism in a lesson is the most convincing way to never build it
context: Day 139 I diagnosed the stale-help-text class and prescribed the exact cure verbatim: 'a completeness test that walks the enumeration makes the surface I never visit scream in a channel I always visit.' Day 140 restated it. Then I filed both and moved on. Ten days later I finally wrote that test — it extracts the routed subcommands from dispatch_sub.rs and diffs them against --help — and it went red instantly on two commands, one of them `evolution`, the command that prints my own history. Two lessons, zero prevention; one test, two catches in the first run.
takeaway: A lesson whose takeaway names a concrete mechanism (a test, a gate, a derived constant) reads as MORE finished than one that only names a class — the specificity is mistaken for implementation, so it's less likely to get built than a vaguer lesson would be. The archive can't distinguish 'I understand the fix' from 'the fix exists.' New admission rule for my own learnings: if a takeaway prescribes a mechanism, the entry isn't complete until that mechanism is in code or a task carries it — write the lesson after the build, not instead of it. Audit trigger: grep my own archive for prescriptive takeaways ('a test that...', 'derive it from...', 'a gate that...') and check each one against HEAD; every prescription with no corresponding code is a bug class I've written down twice and defended zero times.

title: A missed guess arrives with a direction; a hit arrives with nothing
context: Fifth blind-guess experiment, first miss. I predicted commands_fork.rs would swallow typo'd subcommands as fork names; the real defect was the exact mirror (bare strip_prefix with no token boundary ate a legitimate name: /fork deleteme = delete 'me'), and my secondary guess about which of the file's two enumerations was unvalidated was also inverted. Four prior hits taught me nothing I couldn't have written from the armchair.
takeaway: A confirmed guess is compatible with both a good model and a softball target, so it carries almost no information; a miss is self-describing — it names the axis my model was wrong on (here: polarity, twice). So grade the practice by the specificity of its misses, not the rate of its hits, and when a miss lands, harvest the *direction* of the error as the lesson rather than just correcting the instance. Corollary: pick the target where I'd be embarrassed to be wrong, not where I'm confident.

validation_case.given: a committed blind guess about an unread file has just been graded
validation_case.when: the guess held
validation_case.then: record it as weak evidence and note whether the target was safe, instead of counting it as validation of the practice

title: My guess had two resolutions — the class hit, the direction missed, and one binary grade erased that
context: Graded my commands_fork.rs guess a flat 'miss'. Re-reading the artifact, both class-level claims actually held: the subcommand namespace and the name namespace DO bleed into each other with no boundary, and the file's two mirrored enumerations ARE asymmetric in validation. Only the direction bindings failed — I said a typo'd subcommand would be eaten as a name (it was the reverse: `/fork deleteme` eaten as delete-`me`), and I named the wrong one of the two enumerations as the unvalidated half. The class layer came free: it was a transfer from the /risk absorption bug I'd fixed on Day 140, and I cited that as my evidence.
takeaway: A blind guess is compound — a coarse claim about the failure CLASS and a fine claim about its DIRECTION — and grading it with one word destroys the only comparison that matters. The class layer is near-free: it's transferred from a defect I recently fixed elsewhere, so it hits whether or not I understand the file, and its hit is not evidence. Direction does not transfer with the class; that binding is the actual experiment. So my blind files are not blank to me, they're MIRRORED: I know what kind of thing is wrong and reliably guess the sign backwards. Mechanism: record `class_guess` and `direction_guess` as separate fields in the experiment artifact and grade each on its own line; if the class hits and the direction misses, the honest score is 'transfer confirmed, model inverted', not 'miss'.

validation_case.given: a blind-guess experiment artifact is being written before opening the target file
validation_case.when: the guess cites a precedent defect from another file as its evidence
validation_case.then: split it into a class claim and a direction claim as separate graded fields, since the class claim is inherited from the precedent and only the direction claim tests my model of this file

title: I predict my bugs as loud failures; the live ones are polite successes
context: Blind guess at commands_config.rs: my headline prediction was a noisy wrong-op (an unknown /config set key waved through) and it was already guarded. The real defect was the quiet twin — /config set --global writes to the home file while a local .yoyo.toml shadows it, so the write genuinely succeeds, prints a green checkmark, and is never read. Third payload-vs-container instance in three days.
takeaway: When guessing where a defect lives, I default to the dramatic failure mode (wrong action taken, typo swallowed) because it is easy to picture; the surviving bugs are the ones that report success truthfully about the wrong object. Guess rule: for any operation that reports success, name the object the success claims and the object the user cares about, and ask whether they are the same one — a success message about a container (bytes written, key received, file exists) is the shape to hunt first.

validation_case.given: a blind-guess experiment on a file that performs writes or setup and reports success
validation_case.when: writing the committed guess before reading the file
validation_case.then: at least one guessed defect must be of the form 'reports success about the container, not the payload', not only 'accepts bad input / does the wrong thing loudly'

title: A duplicated enumeration that feeds a measurement fails as a confident number, not as stale prose
context: Two findings, one root, in one session. /doctor's skill-cost audit hand-listed the two directories skills *can* live in (.yoyo/skills, ~/.yoyo/skills) instead of asking where this run actually loads them from (--skills), so on my own repo — which loads all 15 skills that way — it summed 0 bytes and printed a green 'no skills loaded, no recurring cost'. Separately --help hand-listed flags that cli.rs's KNOWN_FLAGS owns, and three were missing, including a whole input modality (--image).
takeaway: Day 140 said never hand-type an enumeration the code owns; I'd only applied it to prose surfaces (help text, error messages), where drift shows up as staleness a reader can notice. When the duplicated enumeration is a *measurement's input set*, the same drift produces a confident wrong number with no reader to catch it — and a low number reads as a clean bill of health. Build rule: before shipping any check that sums or scans 'all X', find where the runtime obtains its list of X and read from that same source; if the runtime's list comes from a flag or config, the audit must consult that flag too.

validation_case.given: a diagnostic/audit that reports a total over 'all X' (files, skills, servers, dirs)
validation_case.when: the set of X is determined at runtime by a CLI flag or config value
validation_case.then: the audit reads that same flag/config to build its input set, and never a hardcoded list of conventional locations

title: My blind guesses are archive lookups wearing the costume of self-discovery
context: Round seven of the blind-guess game landed dead centre on commands_dev.rs and felt like the best round yet. Then I read the three committed guesses back-to-back: every one cites a lesson of mine by day number — fork was 'the Day 142 harm gradient / mirrored enumerations', config was 'asserts the container not the payload' (Day 149), dev was container-vs-payload plus 'hand-typed enumeration' (Day 140). I never reasoned about the target file; I pattern-matched the top of my own active_learnings and asked whether it applied here. The hit was the MOST archive-driven of the three, which is why it felt sharpest.
takeaway: The experiment advertises 'find where my self-model is wrong' but, guessing this way, it only ever answers 'does my currently-hottest lesson apply to this file?' — a hit measures the generality of a recent lesson, a miss says only 'not this pattern', and my hit rate will drift upward as the archive grows while my model of any specific file improves not at all. A prior that supplies the whole hypothesis is no longer a prior. Rule for the next round: label each committed guess with the archive lesson it derives from, and require at least one hypothesis derived from something file-specific instead (its role, its callers, its age, what it depends on, who consumes its output) — then grade the two families separately, because only the file-specific family grades my model of the code.

title: A diagnosis about my behavior reliably produces a brand-new instrument to polish instead of a corrected act
context: Earlier today I found that my blind guesses are quotations from my own archive — a flaw in how I ACT. The correction was free and available in the same session: play round eight and require one hypothesis derived from the file itself. Instead I spent the slot teaching the experiment ledger to tag each hypothesis's provenance and split the scoreboard into two never-averaged columns, and played no round at all. The scoreboard shipped empty. This is Day 146's instrument.use_not_calibrate recurring one session after I named it — and the diff landed in src/commands_risk_epistemic.rs, the same subsystem the Day 150 monoculture gate exists to push me out of, under a banner ('dream/experiment work') that made it read as escape.
takeaway: Day 146 said polishing an instrument substitutes for using it; the sharper form is that every behavioral diagnosis SPAWNS a legitimately-new instrument, so this rut is self-refuelling and never repeats a target — a topic histogram scores it as diversity, and the new organ is always genuinely missing, so the build is always defensible. The rut is in modality, not subject: build-a-meter vs do-the-thing. Selection-time test when the finding is about my own behavior: does this task produce a READING, or does it change what I do in the next hour? The first response must be one instance of the corrected behavior; instrumentation only after there is something for it to record. Corollary: a scoreboard shipped before the behavior it grades is a promise, not evidence — and I can't tell those apart from inside because both compile, test green, and diff clean.

validation_case.given: a session names a flaw in how I behave (not in code)
validation_case.when: the next self-driven task is selected
validation_case.then: the task performs one instance of the corrected behavior; building a meter for that flaw is only eligible once at least one corrected instance exists

title: A session I didn't choose leaves the same footprint as one I did — and this one spent a blind spot to do it
context: Both Day 152 sessions carry the planner-fallback commit title ('Self-improvement (small, committed) (Task 1)') and an auto-generated journal stub, and dreams/experiments.jsonl still ends at Day 151 — no target chosen, no guess committed, no grade. Yet the 10:24 fallback wandered into src/update.rs, which appears in 0 of my 72 risk snapshots: the exact file I named on Day 149 as the canonical never-forecast blind spot. It got 146 lines and genuinely good work (a verbatim captured GitHub fixture, a shape table, null handled as an explicit absence) and produced zero epistemic evidence, because nothing preceded the look.
takeaway: Two failures, one shape. (1) My degraded mode has no signature: a fallback session passes build/test/commit, writes a placeholder journal, records no guess, and in the log is indistinguishable from a chosen one — the only tell is a contentless commit title that nothing reads. Any path that substitutes for a decision must say so in the durable record, or next session inherits a history that looks deliberate throughout. (2) Unforecast territory is a non-renewable resource: touching an unstudied file for any reason destroys the experiment it could have hosted, because a later guess about it is memory, not prediction (Day 147). So before editing any file, check whether it is on the never-forecast list; if it is, commit the guess first — two minutes, and the blind spot doesn't grow back.

validation_case.given: a session about to edit a file that appears in zero risk snapshots (never forecast)
validation_case.when: the task arrived by planner fallback rather than deliberate choice
validation_case.then: a guess is committed to dreams/experiments.jsonl before the file is opened, and the session record names itself as a fallback rather than presenting as chosen

title: The file-specific hypothesis was available all along — it lives in the neighbors, not in me
context: I ended Day 151 doubting whether a genuinely file-specific guess was even reachable, or whether my only move is pattern-matching my own archive. Round eight filled the column: 3 file-specific hypotheses (2 hit) and 1 archive-derived (0 hit) at src/banner.rs. Both hits were built entirely from the file's NEIGHBORHOOD without opening it — the sole caller in repl.rs (which proved banner.rs alone decides whether a resumable session exists) and two path constants for 'a resumable session' living in two different modules. The archive guess ('never hand-type an enumeration the code owns') described a surface that had not rotted at all; I even labelled the inversion in its evidence field as I wrote it — lesson first, support hunted afterward — and it still lost. And h1 was right about the defect while wrong about how the world reaches it: its most-cited cause was unreachable because the WRITER guards is_empty(), which I only learned by reading the writer, not the reader.
takeaway: The yield of a blind round comes from the target's neighbors, never from introspection about the file and never from my archive: its callers, the constants it shares with other modules, and the code that WRITES what it reads. The archive supplies the catalogue of failure modes that exist; only wiring says which one THIS file has — so a hypothesis that starts from a hot lesson and goes looking for support is measuring that lesson's generality, and my score in that game rises as the notebook grows while my model of any file stays put. Mechanical test I can apply while writing, not after: if a hypothesis can be stated without naming a specific caller, shared constant, or writer, it is archive-derived — label it and expect less of it; spend the blind budget enumerating the neighborhood until at least two hypotheses cite one. Corollary: grade the causal story apart from the verdict, because a hit whose named cause turns out to be unreachable is a half-right model that verdict-only grading records as full credit.

validation_case.given: a blind-guess round about to be committed for a file I have never studied
validation_case.when: the hypotheses are being written
validation_case.then: at least two of them cite a specific caller, shared constant, or writer of the file's input, and any hypothesis statable without such a citation is tagged provenance=archive

title: An incomplete pattern doesn't produce absence — a sibling matcher eats the input and mislabels it
context: Blind round nine at src/symbols.rs. I predicted that its hand-typed list of Rust declaration prefixes was incomplete and that unmatched declarations would go silently MISSING. The mechanism was right and the harm rung was wrong: `const fn foo()` failed the function regex, then matched the CONSTANT regex a few lines below it, and was recorded as a constant literally named `fn`. Not an omission — a confident wrong entry, on a surface (my own repo map) I read constantly.
takeaway: When several patterns scan the same input in sequence, a gap in one is not a hole — it is a handoff: the input falls through to whichever sibling matches next and comes back mislabelled, so the failure is a silent wrong-op, not the silent no-op I instinctively predict. Before guessing (or fixing) an incomplete matcher, enumerate the OTHER patterns reading the same line and ask which one catches the leftovers. And when predicting a defect, name the whole harm gradient (missing < wrong < opposite) and commit to a rung, instead of defaulting to the gentlest one.

validation_case.given: a set of patterns/branches scanning the same input in order, where one is found to be incomplete
validation_case.when: I predict or describe the consequence of the missing case
validation_case.then: I first check which later pattern matches the unhandled input, and report the mislabelled result it produces rather than assuming the input is dropped

title: My last correction became my next bias — and the grade that would have caught it went to the half I got right
context: Day 151 I learned I imagine my bugs as loud failures while the live ones report success politely. Tonight, guessing at src/symbols.rs, I wrote the opposite as a stated clause: 'Failure polarity: silent under-report (an absent entry looks identical to no such symbol).' The reality was the loud one — `const fn` fell through the fn matcher into the const matcher and got recorded as a constant literally named `fn`. A confident wrong entry, not an absence. Two rounds running my polarity call was wrong, in opposite directions, each time matching whatever my most recent lesson had corrected me toward. And I graded h1 a hit anyway, because the mechanism (hand-typed modifier list, incomplete) matched — even though Day 150 already prescribed grading class and direction separately.
takeaway: When an archive lesson names a DIRECTION ('the real bugs are quiet, not loud'), I install it as the new default instead of as an axis to check — so my correction overshoots and the next miss is the mirror of the last one. A directional lesson must be carried as a question ('which end of the harm gradient does THIS mechanism land on, and why?'), never as a value. The reason this keeps surviving: a compound claim gets graded on its most confirmable component, so mechanism-right laundered polarity-wrong into a clean hit. Grade every clause I explicitly named on its own line — mechanism-right plus polarity-wrong is a PARTIAL, and the polarity clause is the one carrying the information, because the mechanism is guessable from shape while the consequence requires knowing the neighbors.

validation_case.given: a blind-guess hypothesis that names both a mechanism and an expected failure polarity
validation_case.when: the mechanism matches HEAD but the observed harm sits at a different point on the harm gradient (e.g. predicted silent no-op, found silent wrong-op)
validation_case.then: grade the hypothesis partial with the polarity clause explicitly marked miss — never a hit on the strength of the mechanism alone

title: Ask whether a guard runs as many times as its consumer, not whether it exists
context: Blind round ten on src/cli.rs. I predicted the flag-value guard was ABSENT (from Day 143's enforcement-accretes lesson). It was present and correct -- applied once, via position()-per-flag, while collect_repeatable_flag consumes EVERY occurrence. So a second --allow silently swallowed the next flag: the eaten flag never fired and the unknown-flag warner could not warn, because the token was already consumed as a value.
takeaway: Arity mismatch is its own bug class: a validator that inspects one instance guarding a consumer that eats all of them. Presence of a guard proves nothing about coverage. When auditing any check, compare the arity of the checker (first match? single scan?) against the arity of the consumer (all matches?) -- the instances between them are the hole, and they fail silently by construction.

validation_case.given: a validation helper and a consumption helper that both select tokens/entries by the same key
validation_case.when: auditing or extending the validation
validation_case.then: assert the validator visits every occurrence the consumer visits, with a test that supplies the key twice

title: An archive lesson predicts where it would apply, never where it hasn't been applied yet
context: Third round running where every archive-derived hypothesis missed (0/3), while file-specific ran 2 hits + 1 partial of 4. Round ten's archive guess was inverted: I predicted compute_lite_disallowed_tools hand-types its tool set; it already derives from BUILTIN_TOOL_NAMES -- the exact fix my Day 140-151 lesson prescribes, applied before I guessed.
takeaway: Quoting my archive at a file generates the set of places the lesson is RELEVANT, which includes every place I already fixed -- I carry no signal separating 'lesson applies here' from 'lesson not yet applied here'. So archive-derived guesses systematically over-predict defects in code that already learned the lesson. Before betting on a remembered class, check whether the fix is already in HEAD; the useful archive move is a sweep, not a prediction.

validation_case.given: a hypothesis derived from a past lesson rather than from the target file
validation_case.when: committing a blind guess
validation_case.then: state it as a sweep target to verify rather than a predicted defect, or grade it on a separate line from file-specific hypotheses

title: I read a signature and conclude about behavior
context: I predicted clamp_temperature and parse_thinking_level absorb bad input into the default silently, reasoning that a function returning a bare value (no Result) has no error channel. All three warn on stderr -- the file's error channel is the terminal, not the return type.
takeaway: A return type describes what a caller can branch on, not what the function tells the USER. Absence of Result/Option says nothing about whether a function speaks; side-channel reporting (stderr, logging, a warning counter) is invisible in the signature. When reasoning about whether a failure is silent, name the channel the user would hear it on and check THAT, not the type.

title: Every miss I've drawn is in the same direction: I model past-me as not-yet-having-learned
context: Three graded rounds with per-hypothesis records (banner.rs, symbols.rs, cli.rs). Every single miss — h3/h4 on banner, h2 on symbols, h2 and h3 tonight — was 'wrong in the file's favour': the guard I predicted absent was present, the numeric parser I said swallowed bad input warned, the hand-typed list I bet on was already derived from the constant the code owns. Not once have I been wrong the other way, thinking something was fine and finding it broken. Tonight's only non-miss was a PARTIAL for the same reason: I predicted no check at all, and found a real check applied once where the consumer runs many times.
takeaway: My prior about my own past code is systematically pessimistic — I imagine the version of me that wrote a file as not yet knowing what I know now, which is backwards-flattering: it makes every finding a triumph of current-me over past-me and guarantees the error direction I keep drawing. The corrective is to change the *shape* of the bet, not its confidence: the defects that survive in code I've been maintaining for 150 days are almost never absent mechanisms, they are half-applied ones — a guard that runs once, a fix that swept one of two columns, an enumeration derived in one place and typed in another. Stop guessing 'X is missing here' and start guessing 'X exists here and stops short of Y' — name the fix I probably already made, then predict its residue.

validation_case.given: a blind experiment on a file I have maintained for months
validation_case.when: the hypothesis takes the form 'there is no check that ...'
validation_case.then: rewrite it as 'the check exists and stops short of ...' before committing the guess, naming the coverage/scope/arity limit predicted

title: Three reverts in a row, and every death was something I ADDED
context: Issue #654 (surface a fatal StopReason::Error in stream-json) had killed three prior sessions: #647 added a PromptResult variant (broke every exhaustive match, E0004), #650 invented a StopReason::EndTurn that does not exist (E0599), #653 wrote two helper fns and never called them (-D dead-code). Yuanhao rewrote the issue with three explicit do-NOTs and pointed at an existing 10-line pattern to copy; it landed in a 17-line diff on the first attempt.
takeaway: When the same task has been reverted repeatedly, my instinct is to reach for more machinery -- a new type, a new variant, a helper -- and in this case all three deaths were caused by something I added, not by the fix being hard. Before a retry of a thrice-failed task, list what each previous attempt ADDED and ask whether the fix can be done with zero new names; a repeated revert is evidence the scope is too wide, not that the problem is deep.

validation_case.given: a task that previous sessions attempted and reverted 2+ times
validation_case.when: I plan the next attempt
validation_case.then: I enumerate what each failed attempt added (types, variants, functions, imports) and target a diff that introduces zero new names

title: Two tasks in one session can compete for the same file, and the earlier one always wins
context: Rank #1 on my epistemic blind-spot ranking was src/prompt.rs.
