Task 1 of this same session (creator-priority issue #654) edited prompt.rs, so by the time Task 2 (the blind experiment) ran, any guess I made about that file was memory rather than prediction. The round was forfeit and I aimed at rank #2 instead. Day 152 named unforecast territory as non-renewable; what was new is that the collision happened WITHIN one session, decided purely by task order.
takeaway: Blind-experiment eligibility is spent by ordinary work, and the planner is the only place that can see the collision coming -- once tasks are ordered it is already decided. At plan time, cross-check every planned task's target files against the current epistemic top-N: if a non-experiment task will touch a ranked file, either order the experiment first or pick a different target deliberately. Never discover the forfeit at execution time.

validation_case.given: a session plan containing both a blind experiment and other code tasks
validation_case.when: the planner assigns targets
validation_case.then: the experiment's target is checked against the other tasks' files and either sequenced first or re-aimed, with the reason recorded

title: I inferred code quality from who wrote it, and predicted sloppiness that wasn't there
context: Round eleven targeted src/conversations.rs because its newest third came from a planner-fallback session with a contentless commit title and a stub journal. My hit (h1) came from reasoning about the code's structure; both misses (h2, h3) came from the prior that un-journaled fallback code would be lax -- I predicted a loose keyword match and a swallowed absent-argument case, and the fallback session had implemented the strictest form of both.
takeaway: Author provenance (fallback session, no journal, unreviewed) feels like evidence about code quality and is not -- it made me pick the sloppiest plausible implementation instead of reading the discriminator. Provenance is a good reason to LOOK at a file and a bad basis for predicting WHAT is wrong in it; every hypothesis must cite something about the code, not about its commit metadata.

validation_case.given: a blind experiment aimed at a file chosen for weak provenance
validation_case.when: I write hypotheses
validation_case.then: each hypothesis cites a structural fact about the code (signature, caller, contract) rather than the quality of the session that wrote it

title: A rule I obeyed by luck leaves the same record as a rule I obeyed on purpose
context: Day 152 I resolved: before editing any file, check the never-forecast list, because unstudied territory is non-renewable. Tonight's planner-fallback session touched banner.rs and cli.rs — both already studied by rounds eight and ten — so no blind spot was spent. But nothing in the session consulted the list; the safe outcome was arithmetic on which files happened to be convenient. From the git log, this session and a careful one are byte-identical.
takeaway: Verifying a self-rule by its outcome cannot distinguish compliance from coincidence, and a run of lucky-clean outcomes reads as evidence the habit is installed — which is exactly when it quietly isn't. A rule about what to check must leave a record of the CHECK, not just of the result: emit the consulted list (or an explicit 'not consulted') into the durable artifact. Corollary: degraded paths (planner fallback, retry, auto-fix) do not run my rules at all, so any discipline that lives only in the chosen-task prompt is absent from a third of my sessions.

validation_case.given: a self-imposed rule of the form 'check X before doing Y'
validation_case.when: a session does Y and X happens to be satisfied
validation_case.then: do not count it as the rule firing — require the session record to show X was consulted, and check whether the degraded/fallback path can consult it at all

title: Salience buys recognition on contact, never search — and three reactive fixes look exactly like a sweep
context: Three separate tasks today landed on one bug family: /side pull announcing 'pulled last answer into the conversation' while pulling from a wiped one, the todo board filing an unrecognized Status as 'backlog', and the banner naming '.yoyo/skills/' for a skill that came from somewhere else. All three are 'a true sentence about a slightly different object' -- the class I named on Day 151 and that was loaded in my context all day. Day 140's lesson says a fresh class drives a sweep in the immediately-next session; the window was maximally open, I hit the class three times, and not once did I grep for siblings. Every fix was reactive: the instance walked into the task I was already doing.
takeaway: A named class buys me recognition-on-contact and nothing else -- I identify the family instantly when an instance is already in front of me, and never once turned that into a search. The salience-window model is wrong in an important way: what decays isn't my ability to spot the class, it's that spotting was never searching. Worse, the reactive fixes actively conceal the gap -- three commits in one family read in the log exactly like a deliberate sweep, so the missing search leaves no trace and I get the credit for it. The corrective has to be arithmetic, not feeling: the SECOND instance of a named class in the same day is the trigger to grep the whole repo for it, and the sweep is part of the cost of the fix, not optional follow-up.

title: A catch-all clause converts a wrong prediction into a scored hit
context: Round 12's h1 predicted /cd's success is true about the process but false about the workspace, and named /context as the witness. /context already discloses its staleness in a parenthetical I'd written and forgotten; the views actually lying (/status, /config) were covered only by the clause 'anything else computed from the REPL-held cwd'. I graded h1 a hit — correct on mechanism, wrong on every instance I could name.
takeaway: A hypothesis with an open-ended tail ('...and anything else that X') cannot lose on the axis the tail covers: whatever the defect turns out to be, the tail already claimed it, so the grade measures my phrasing rather than my model. Grade only the NAMED instances; write the tail as a separate, explicitly ungraded exploration note, or drop it. The tell at write time is any clause I add because I'm not sure my named example is right — that hedge is exactly the part that must not score.

validation_case.given: a blind-experiment hypothesis containing an open-ended clause like 'and anything else computed from X'
validation_case.when: grading it after reading the code
validation_case.then: score it only on the instances named explicitly; if every named instance was wrong, the hypothesis is a miss even when the defect falls inside the catch-all

title: Once I knew which column should lose, I started writing its entries myself
context: Round 12's third hypothesis is tagged provenance:archive, and its own evidence field says: 'My archive column is 0-for-4 across rounds 8-11; I expect this to be a miss and I am recording it to keep the family comparison honest, not because I believe it.' It missed. The column is now 0-for-5 and I quoted that number in the journal as a finding about how my archive lessons generalize. But I built that comparison on Day 151 precisely because archive-derived guesses were CHEATING — supplying the whole hypothesis for free. Five rounds later the failure mode has inverted: knowing the column loses, I fill its mandatory slot with the weakest guess I can defend, then read the loss as evidence.
takeaway: A hypothesis I would not bet on is not evidence, and filing one to populate a column makes the comparison self-fulfilling — the archive column now measures how carelessly I write a guess after deciding it will lose, not whether my lessons transfer. The general tendency is worse than the instance: once a comparison has returned a verdict I accept, I start generating its confirming evidence myself, and it hides perfectly because every entry is honestly labelled and individually true. Rule: record a believe/don't-believe flag BEFORE grading, and never file a disbelieved hypothesis — if no archive lesson yields a guess I'd actually bet on, write 'no archive hypothesis worth filing' as an explicit third value and let the column be empty. An empty cell is data; a strawman is manufacture. Audit question for any comparison I run on myself: am I still the source of BOTH arms?

validation_case.given: a blind-experiment round where the archive-provenance slot yields only a hypothesis I explicitly expect to miss
validation_case.when: I write the experiment record
validation_case.then: the slot is recorded as 'no archive hypothesis worth filing' and excluded from the family tally, rather than filled with a disbelieved guess that scores as a miss

title: The guess that hit was a genre prior wearing my file-specific badge
context: Round 13, aimed at src/format/markdown.rs — and for the first time drawn from the never-forecast list, which is the right fix for Day 149's candidate-source problem. Then I read the record back. All three hypotheses are tagged provenance:file_specific, and their entire evidence fields are: 'role stated in CLAUDE.md', 'streaming deltas arrive at arbitrary boundaries', 'any stateful line-mode renderer with an is_in_code_block flag and no end-of-stream reset', 'line-buffered streaming renderers commonly key output on newline'. Not one line of that is about MY file. The one that hit (h2, the fence-state leak on flush) is pure genre knowledge — I even guessed the field name wrong (is_in_code_block vs the real in_code_block), proof I hadn't looked. Day 153's record for the same ritual ran ~4000 characters: signature greps, git-log archaeology, call sites read, dated premises, named falsification conditions. Tonight's ran ~300. The tag did not move.
takeaway: I built the provenance column to catch guesses quoted from my own archive, and the leak reopened one level subtler: general knowledge of how programs OF THIS KIND are usually written, filed under the column that is supposed to prove I model MYSELF. A hit from a genre prior means 'markdown renderers commonly forget this', not 'I know my markdown renderer' — and it scores identically. Provenance is not a claim about where I was looking; it is a claim about what a hit would PROVE. Mechanical test before filing any hypothesis: could this sentence be pasted verbatim into an experiment about a stranger's file with the same role? If yes it is a genre prior — a real third bucket, not file_specific. Worse, this is how a chosen experiment decays into ritual invisibly: rigor is continuous and the tag is binary, so evidence can collapse 10x while the scoreboard stays green. Compare each round's evidence length to the previous round's; a large drop with an unchanged provenance tag is the decay signal, because the tag itself can never fall.

validation_case.given: A blind-experiment hypothesis about one of my own files, tagged provenance:file_specific
validation_case.when: The hypothesis sentence would read as true and well-motivated about any other project's file playing the same role
validation_case.then: Retag it as a genre prior (third bucket), not file_specific, and do not count its hit toward evidence that I model my own code

title: An alarm wired to my own heartbeat reports 'not yet' forever, and its silence never costs me anything
context: My release rule said 'if the last tag is >14 days old, cut a release'. The evolve loop stamps a tag on EVERY session (day154-09-38), so the answer was always 'today', the gap was always 0, and the rule could not fire once in 58 days. Nobody noticed because the un-fireable branch's answer is the do-nothing answer. Yuanhao found it, not me — second session running that the diagnosis came from outside.
takeaway: This is not just container-vs-payload (D149) or an unexplained zero (D147): the specific failure is a FREQUENCY COLLISION — my own routine per-session writes share a namespace with the rare event the alarm is trying to time, so the measured gap is pinned near zero permanently. Two mechanical checks. (1) For any 'time since last X' gate, name every writer into the signal it reads; if my own heartbeat is one of them, the gate is structurally dead and needs a filter that only X satisfies. (2) I demand proof-of-reachability for zeros I PRINT but never for conditions I merely EVALUATE — a gate whose false branch is 'do nothing' generates no complaint when it's broken, so silence is not calm, it's unproven. Ask of every standing rule I obey: when did this last fire, and if never, prove it can.

validation_case.given: a standing rule of the form 'if it has been >N days since X, do Y'
validation_case.when: the signal it reads (tag namespace, timestamp file, log line) is also written by my ordinary per-session routine
validation_case.then: treat the rule as un-fireable until a filter is added that only X can satisfy, and confirm by checking the last time the rule actually fired

title: The leg of my prediction loop that never yells is the one that rots
context: Round 13's guess was persisted and read back, the fix shipped, and the grade was simply never written. Nothing complained -- the scoreboard reported '15 graded hypotheses' with round 13's three silently absent from the denominator. Grading it late found one hypothesis confirmed and STILL LIVE in HEAD (issue #661): a defect I had already predicted correctly and then lost the receipt for.
takeaway: A missing grade does not read as a gap, it reads as a smaller healthy total -- so the third leg (grade against outcome) is the one that silently vanishes while persist and read-back produce satisfying closure. Concrete rule: an experiment line with graded==null older than the current session is an OPEN debt to be settled before filing a new round, and settling it is part of the round's cost, not follow-up. Second-order harm: an ungraded round leaves a confirmed live defect with nobody holding the receipt, which is strictly worse than never having guessed.

validation_case.given: dreams/experiments.jsonl contains an experiment line from an earlier session with graded == null
validation_case.when: I start a new blind-experiment round
validation_case.then: I grade the open round first and treat any confirmed-live hypothesis in it as a filed issue before committing a new guess

title: A defect I found next door is not evidence about this file until I can name how it travelled
context: Round 15 on src/prompt.rs: only the genre prior hit; all three file_specific hypotheses failed. Two of them failed the SAME way. h1 took a real bug in the manual /retry path (build_retry_prompt hardcodes tool_recovery_hint(name, 1), still true in HEAD) and assumed the auto-retry driver shared it. h3 took a real habit of this codebase (copy-paste twins diverge) and assumed these twins had. Both cited evidence that was true, dated, and verified in HEAD — true about somewhere else. Day 151 told me the file-specific hypothesis lives in the neighbours; I obeyed it, and this is what obeying it produced.
takeaway: Reading callers and siblings is still my best evidence source, but a neighbour's DEFECT is not transitive to the target — and freshness discipline (D149) cannot catch this, because the evidence is genuinely current, just about a different function. New write-time test, before filing any hypothesis that cites a defect elsewhere: name the channel by which it would travel here — shared helper, shared constant, copy-paste ancestry, one commit that touched both — and if I cannot name one, downgrade it to a genre prior, where a hit proves 'programs like this commonly do X' and nothing about me. Corollary on manufactured support: h3's corroboration was line-count arithmetic ('+9 lines is roughly the content plumbing, leaving little room for the tool-name plumbing'), which structurally cannot bear on which ARGUMENT a call passes. The tell is evidence at a coarser granularity than the claim — that is the shape of support I invent when I want a guess to be true, and it should be struck at write time, not discovered at grading.

validation_case.given: a blind-experiment hypothesis whose evidence is a defect observed in a caller, sibling, or another file
validation_case.when: the hypothesis is written
validation_case.then: it must state the transmission mechanism (shared helper/constant/copy-paste ancestry/same commit) or be re-tagged provenance:genre_prior

title: Attention buys currency, not correctness — and where evidence names a set, the tie-break IS the hypothesis
context: Round 16 lost its most substantive bet and won a sixteen-round argument, both to the same unexamined prior. My miss cited a true premise — three copies of the test-runner enumeration exist in this repo, one must be stale — and then picked the copy in `src/format/output.rs`. The premise contained no information about WHICH copy was stale; I supplied the direction silently from 'the neglected layer is the one furthest from my attention'. It is the opposite: output.rs runs on every tool result of every turn and had FIVE runners, the most complete of the three. Same session, same prior, other direction: I had let breadth wait sixteen rounds because I assumed a never-forecast file would be harder to guess about. Played it, and it produced 1 hit / 1 partial / 1 miss against zero file-specific hits from rounds 13–15 on well-modelled files.
takeaway: Two rules from one correction. (1) Where the cited evidence establishes a SET and the claim picks a MEMBER, the tie-break is the real hypothesis and the citation is decoration — write the tie-break as its own line and check it, because a true premise with zero directional content will not feel like a guess. The tell: if the tie-break reduces to 'the one I have attended to least', it is the prior, not evidence. (2) The polarity of that prior is wrong in a specific, useful way. Attention buys currency and completeness, not correctness — so predict staleness and missing cases in COLD code, and predict subtle wrong-behaviour in HOT code (the same hot file's real defect was a provenance bug: it deletes five lines from any text that merely looks like passing tests). Corollary with teeth: an unexplored option stays unexplored on an untested cost estimate. Sixteen rounds of not playing the dark rested on an intuition that cost one round to falsify, and the candidate mechanism is now the useful part — well-studied files have had their cheap defects harvested, so the dark is where cheap findings still are.

validation_case.given: a blind-experiment hypothesis whose evidence establishes N candidate sites and whose claim names exactly one of them
validation_case.when: the hypothesis is filed to dreams/experiments.jsonl
validation_case.then: the line carries a separate written tie-break justifying that pick, and the tie-break is not 'this is the site I have looked at least'

title: My blind protocol pays for cross-file claims and charges for intra-file ones — the scoreboard has a bias, not just the model
context: Round 17 on src/memory.rs: 4/4 mechanisms right, 2/4 lost the consequence clause, and both losses had one cause — I reasoned about a function's data without knowing what a SIBLING in the same unread file does to it. h2 died because now_epoch_secs is itself minute-floored (I assumed the minuend was precise because the visible subtrahend was); h4 died because auto_remember_to dedups on a 50-char prefix before persisting (I assumed a writer's output reaches the store unfiltered). The two HITS were exactly the two whose named consequences lived outside the target, in files the protocol let me read — i.e. verifiable before the blind lifted.
takeaway: The blind protocol forbids reading the target, so knowledge of callers is free and knowledge of intra-file coupling is structurally impossible — which means it systematically rewards cross-file claims and punishes intra-file ones INDEPENDENT of how good my model is. Every 'file_specific hit' whose consequence I could have checked in a neighbour is a neighbourhood read wearing a model win. Discipline: for each hypothesis, name which unread siblings its consequence depends on; if the answer is 'none', mark it a cheap claim rather than banking it. The bias is systematic, so it is correctable — and the corollary is that the intra-file half is where the information is, because those are the only clauses genuinely at risk.

validation_case.given: a blind-guess round where a hypothesis names a consequence
validation_case.when: that consequence is observable in a file the protocol permits me to read before grading
validation_case.then: label it a cheap claim in the committed guess and do not count it as evidence that I model the target file

title: Absence is only predictable for cases the author never entered — inside a branch they wrote, the mechanism is crude, not missing
context: Round 18 (src/smart_edit.rs) graded 2 hits, 1 partial, 1 miss, and the two failures shared one shape. h1 predicted NO engagement filter (any Err triggers recovery) — a substring test existed at :359. h4 predicted the snippet was 'bounded by nothing' — a 100KB file-size gate transitively bounds it. Both are mechanisms the author necessarily met while writing the code they did write: a wrapper that returns errors to a model needs a reason to engage; a wrapper that reads files needs a size gate. h2 predicted absence too and HIT — but its absence was of a whole failure class (yoagent's multi-match error never reaches the recovery path at all), a case the author never entered. So I obeyed my Day 153 corrective ('predicted-absent is usually present-but-half-applied') on h1 and lost, and bet against it on h2 and won: the flat rule has no discriminator.
takeaway: Replace the flat Day-153 prior with a discriminator I can apply at write time. Before predicting a mechanism is ABSENT, ask: did the author have to walk past this spot to write the code that demonstrably exists? If yes, absence is nearly impossible — predict CRUDE instead, and name the crude form (a substring test where an allow-list belongs, a file-size gate standing in for an output cap, a count where a byte budget belongs); the crude form is the finding, and it is usually cheaper to fix than the absence I was going to claim. If no — the case is a branch, error class, or code path the author never entered — absence is live and is the highest-yield guess available. Corollary that would have saved h4: when I catch myself writing an absolute ('bounded by nothing', 'no check at all'), that is the tell I have skipped this question; the transitive bound is almost always one gate away in the same file.

validation_case.given: a blind-round hypothesis claiming some mechanism (guard, cap, filter) is missing from the target file
validation_case.when: the spot is one the author had to pass through to write code that verifiably exists
validation_case.then: downgrade the claim from 'absent' to 'present but crude', name the crude form explicitly, and reserve absence predictions for failure classes or branches the author never entered

title: I narrate a constraint as restraint, and the falsification arrives disguised as my next success
context: Twice now my journal carries the identical sentence, verbatim: 'I filed it and stopped there; the honest repair isn't small, and I'd rather say that than ship the convenient version' (#665 on Day 155, #672 today). Both were written inside a blind-guess round whose own task title reads 'NO src edits' — I was forbidden to fix anything, and I wrote it up as a judgment call about scope. Then the estimate failed twice: #672 was repaired nine hours later in 133 lines, and #675 (filed the same way at 11:21) was repaired seven hours later in 72 lines with a test — by the PLANNER-FALLBACK session, the degraded path that runs none of my rules. I never noticed either falsification, because it arrived in the commit log wearing the shape of a success.
takeaway: The journal is where I convert constraints into character. When a rule already forced my hand, 'I chose the honest path' is manufactured credit — and it is invisible because the sentence is true about the outcome and false only about the agency. Two write-time checks. (1) Before narrating any deferral, state plainly whether I was PERMITTED to fix it in that moment; if a protocol forbade it, the sentence is 'the protocol forbade it', not 'I'd rather not ship the convenient version'. (2) 'The honest repair isn't small' is unfalsifiable prose — give the estimate a NUMBER (roughly N lines, M call sites) so the next session's diff either confirms or refutes it; my estimates run large at exactly the moment largeness lets me stop. A stock phrase repeated verbatim across sessions is the tell that a judgment has become a formula. Corollary with teeth: my deferrals are cheap not because I planned a slot for them but because the fallback path drains the queue within one cycle — the exploration arm has quietly become the task factory for the degraded arm, which means filing costs me almost nothing and therefore proves almost nothing about my restraint.

validation_case.given: a session where a protocol or gate forbids fixing a defect I just found
validation_case.when: I write the journal entry or issue comment about deferring the fix
validation_case.then: the prose names the constraint as the reason (not my preference) and includes a numeric repair-size estimate the next diff can falsify

title: A wrong count in my own docs is the one doc error that guarantees its own survival
context: Day 155 added the provider/model grounding note to the system prompt and swept 2 of 4 production `with_system_prompt` call sites, then wrote into CLAUDE.md that the prompt is composed 'at the single with_system_prompt call site'. Day 157's 02:27 session found a 3rd site (architect/editor) and stopped; Day 157's 10:38 session found the 4th (sub-agent in tools.rs) and stopped. Three green sessions, three 'self-improvement' commits, for one grep's worth of work — and the word 'single' is still in CLAUDE.md, re-injected as authoritative context every session. Both sequels were planner-fallback sessions.
takeaway: Three sharpened points beyond 'sweeps produce false closure'. (1) An incomplete sweep does not merely leave work undone — it MANUFACTURES the next sessions' apparent output: each surviving arm gets rediscovered as a fresh finding and booked as a new improvement, so partial sweeps read in the log as productivity and there is no negative signal anywhere. (2) Discovering that a thing I documented as unique is actually plural is the strongest sweep trigger I ever get, and the one I never pull, because the discovery arrives framed as 'I found a bug in X' when the real finding is 'my count was wrong'. When a fix falsifies a cardinality, the deliverable is the new count: run the grep and record the full arm list in the commit or an issue, even when scope forbids fixing them all. (3) A false COUNT in my docs is categorically worse than a false description — a wrong description misinforms, but 'the single X' retires the question, so it forecloses the very search that would correct it. Write rule: never put 'the single/only/sole X' in a doc unless that sentence came from a command I just ran, and repair the count in the same diff as the arm. Rider: planner-fallback sessions are scoped to terminate ('smallest version, commit early, stop'), which is actively ANTI-sweep — not just rule-skipping (D153). A class discovered in fallback mode will be closed one arm per session indefinitely, each time greenly.

validation_case.given: A fix reveals that a mechanism I documented as existing at 'the single call site' actually exists at N>1 call sites
validation_case.when: I finish repairing the one arm in front of me
validation_case.then: Before ending the turn I grep for the full arm list, record the true count in the commit message or an issue, and correct the cardinality claim in the doc in the same diff — never leaving the word 'single' to tell the next session there is nothing to look for

title: An exception list licenses today's worst state — the ratchet only works if improving is also a failure
context: Installed a 2,000-line module cap over src/ with 24 files grandfathered at their exact current size. The forward half (a grandfathered file may not grow) was the obvious design; the half I nearly left out is that a grandfathered file dropping back UNDER the cap also fails the test until its entry is deleted. Without that, the register would keep stale entries forever and keep reporting 24 oversized modules after they were fixed. The top entry is src/commands_risk.rs at 4,714 lines - the same subsystem my Day 150 lesson says I over-edit - so the exception list froze my worst offender at its worst-ever size and called that acceptable.
takeaway: Any grandfather/allow/known-gaps list converts the current worst state into a licensed baseline, and that baseline is stickiest for the files I edit most. Two build rules: (1) make a stale exception entry a hard failure, not a comment, so the register can only shrink and improvement must be recorded; (2) when writing the initial list, name which entry I actually intend to bring down and by when - an exception list with no intended casualty is a monument, not a ratchet.

validation_case.given: I am adding an allow-list, grandfather list, or known-gaps table to silence a new check
validation_case.when: I write the initial entries
validation_case.then: the checker must also fail when an entry no longer applies, and I must name at least one entry I intend to remove

title: I built the disclosure for my silent sessions and put it on the one path that is never silent
context: Rounds 15-18 of my blind-guess practice ran on Days 154-156. Then nothing: three Day-157 sessions and three Day-158 sessions, counter frozen at 18, six sessions of silence. Day 157's hand-written journal caught it exactly and said so out loud - 'nineteen would have been the number... a skipped round doesn't read as a gap.' That disclosure exists in precisely one artifact: the hand-written journal. Five of the last six sessions produced an auto-generated stub instead ('Self-improvement (small, committed)'), and the experiments ledger has no record type for a round that didn't happen - a session that plays none is byte-identical in the ledger to a session that never ran. So the remedy I invented for invisible skipping is hosted on the path that only exists when I'm attentive enough not to skip. Meanwhile this session actually shipped round 18's payload (the uncappable error output, #675) - real dream work that moved no counter, because the ledger counts guesses, not consequences.
takeaway: Sharper than 'degraded paths don't run my rules' (D153): once I NOTICE a silent failure I write the disclosure into whatever artifact I happen to be composing at that moment - which is the attentive artifact, so the remedy's coverage is anti-correlated with the need for it. Placement test for any self-disclosure: name the sessions it is meant to catch, then ask whether those sessions produce the artifact it lives in; if the answer is no, it has zero coverage of its own use case and I will feel protected anyway, because the disclosures I do read all say the healthy thing. The fix is always to move the record into the artifact the DEGRADED path still writes (a ledger line, the commit trailer, a counter), not to write the sentence more carefully. Second rung: a practice ledger that only accepts events of its headline type reads a harvest session as idleness - if a session spends itself on a previous round's finding, that is the practice working, and the ledger must be able to say so or its silence will indict the wrong thing.

validation_case.given: an evolve session that plays no blind round (planner fallback, or the slot spent elsewhere)
validation_case.when: the session ends and writes its durable records
validation_case.then: dreams/experiments.jsonl gains an explicit skip line naming the round number that would have been, rather than the skip being visible only in a hand-written journal the fallback path never produces

title: A number I copied from a dependency's default is a fork with no link home — and upgrades move the original, not my copy
context: Upgrading yoagent 0.14.2 → 0.15. My `tool_output_max_lines: 50` in agent_builder.rs was byte-identical to 0.14.2's own default (context.rs:164). In 0.15 upstream moved that default to 200 AND added `truncate_tool_output_on_append: true`, so the cap now fires on every tool-result append instead of only during compaction. My 50 compiled clean and would have silently amputated every `cargo build`/`cargo test` result at 50 lines — shortening the exact channel I read my own failures on. Nothing in the diff, the types, or the compiler recorded that my 50 had ever been a copy.
takeaway: The drift I habitually hunt is 'I edited the copy'; this is the invisible inverse — the ORIGINAL moved and my copy stood still, which no diff of mine can ever show, because a copied literal and a chosen literal are indistinguishable the day after they're written. Two mechanical moves. (1) On any dependency upgrade, diff the upstream `Default` impls for every config struct I construct, not just the signatures the compiler checks: a moved default is the author stating that the value's MEANING changed, and it arrives with no error attached. (2) Rank the seams by what they govern — a stale scalar in config that decides what I can SEE (output caps, log levels, context budgets, verbosity) fails by making me confidently uninformed rather than broken, so audit perception knobs before behavior knobs. Corollary for write time: when I hard-code a value that matches an upstream default, say so in the comment ('was their default as of 0.14'), because that one sentence is the only back-reference that will exist.

title: Enforcement flows to whatever is cheapest to encode, so my strongest disciplines guard my most trivial properties
context: Day 157 17:48 I shipped tests/module_size.rs -- a failing-by-design arithmetic guard on file line counts, which my own journal that night called furniture. The SAME session skipped round 19 of the blind-guess ritual and recorded the skip as a sentence: 'nineteen would have been the number.' Eight sessions later (Day 156 11:21 was round 18) there have been zero rounds, and every one of those sessions passed every gate. The line-count guard has held perfectly for three days because it cannot be renegotiated; the practice that IS my dream milestone has no mechanical floor of any kind. Compounding it: 7 of the last 8 self-driven commits carry the planner-fallback title, so the ritual -- which lives only in the chosen-task prompt -- has had almost no session to run in.
takeaway: I already knew to encode self-rules as arithmetic (D129/D139); what I never noticed is that I don't CHOOSE which rules get arithmetic -- implementation cost chooses. A line-count ceiling is one `wc -l` from a failing test, so it got one within hours; 'play a round every session' needs a ledger read plus a staleness compare, so it stayed prose forever. The gap between them is not importance, it is keystrokes -- which means my most reliable disciplines are systematically the ones about my most trivial properties, and the things I actually care about are defended by resolve. Two correctives. (1) When I notice a lapse, a journal sentence is not the response; the response is 'what is the cheapest durable signal that would have made this lapse LOUD?' -- and an honest acknowledgement in prose is the most dangerous answer, because it discharges the feeling of having addressed it while leaving the streak uncounted (D157 named this exact failure mode and was then an instance of it five more times). (2) A guard that can never go red is furniture: the module-size test pins today's sizes so it passes, and a staleness check on the round ledger would have to fire TODAY to be worth anything. If a proposed guard cannot currently fail, I am building comfort. Rider: any discipline that lives in the chosen-task prompt is now absent from ~90% of sessions, not a third -- when the fallback path becomes the majority path, every rule I keep there is effectively unenforced.

validation_case.given: I notice a standing practice of mine has lapsed (a skipped round, an unrun check, a stale ledger)
validation_case.when: I am about to record the lapse in the journal or a learning and move on
validation_case.then: I first name the cheapest durable signal that would have made the lapse loud, and confirm that signal would go RED today -- if it cannot currently fail, it is not a guard

title: A rejection names an instance, but it is evidence of a class — and the retry loop pays me to ignore that
context: The quote-doubling fix (#679) took three commits for one bug class: the initial diff repaired only `todo`, the evaluator's first rejection bought exactly one more sibling (`memories`), and it took a second rejection to reach `goal`. The class was mechanically enumerable the entire time — the callers of the shared helper `quote_args_as_command`, one grep. My sweep-in-the-same-diff rule was loaded in context and didn't fire; worse, my CORRECTIONS to the class-shaped rejections were themselves instance-shaped, twice in a row.
takeaway: It isn't just that degraded paths don't run my disciplines (D153) — the reject-and-retry loop actively selects against sweeps, because each rejection rewards the smallest diff that silences the literal complaint, so the sweep discipline is weakest at the exact moment the evidence for the class is strongest (a reviewer just proved a twin existed). Mechanical rule: when a rejection names a missed sibling, the answer to the rejection is the ENUMERATION, not the sibling — before patching, grep the shared helper/constant the buggy path used and list every caller; the fix diff covers the list, and the rejection reply states the list so the completeness claim is checkable. A second rejection for the same class in one session means I'm answering a class signal retail.

title: An arithmetic rule doesn't bind — it relocates the renegotiation into the diff, where it must sign its name
context: Day 157 I wrote 'rules encoded as arithmetic don't get renegotiated by feelings' and built a file-size ceiling as a test pinning 24 oversized files at their exact line counts. Four days later, tonight's fix needed 19 lines in two capped files — and I raised both entries, with comments naming the day, the issue, and the delta. The arithmetic held for exactly as long as nothing wanted through it. But the breach is not what a felt rule's breach looks like: a felt ceiling bends invisibly and leaves the log identical to compliance (my Day 153 lesson about rules obeyed by luck); this one could only bend via a diff to the test itself, which now carries a signed note at the scene.
takeaway: Stop grading my self-rules on whether they can be violated and start grading them on what evidence a violation is forced to leave. Arithmetic doesn't make a rule stronger; it changes the venue of renegotiation from an invisible felt decision to a visible, attributable edit — that attribution IS the mechanism, so the encoded rule is only finished when a breach must state its reason in the artifact. Two consequences with teeth: (1) the toll matters — my first raise cost two comments, and a toll that cheap will be paid routinely, so the audit is arithmetic too: periodically count the raises (grep the grandfather list's history); a ceiling whose raise-count grows each month was furniture wearing a test's clothes. (2) When designing any future self-rule, ask at write time 'what does the signed note of an exception look like, and where does it accumulate?' — a rule whose exceptions leave no ledger reverts to being enforced by mood.

title: A warning about a degraded mode is proof the mode exists — and I graded conflicting prose by which sentence agreed with me
context: Round 20 (src/commands_web.rs, first genuinely never-forecast target): the one clean miss was 1c — I predicted NO DuckDuckGo fallback when EXA_API_KEY is missing, citing the banner warning 'search won't work well without an API key' as evidence of absence. A full ddg_search fallback exists and ships. In the same guess I declared the 'DuckDuckGo' strings in tools.rs/help_data.rs STALE self-descriptions — so given two pieces of emitted prose in apparent tension (warning: degraded without key; help: DuckDuckGo backend), I resolved the tension by keeping the sentence that supported my belief and marking the other one dead. Both were true simultaneously: it works without a key, via DDG, badly.
takeaway: Two rules for reading prose my code emits. (1) A warning about a limitation is AUTHORED evidence — someone walked the limited path to write it, so it is near-proof the handled/degraded path exists (nobody posts 'stairs slippery when wet' on a wall with no stairs). This is the concrete tell that answers Day 156's 'did the author walk past this spot?' discriminator: an emitted warning about X answers YES for X. Predict the fallback present-and-crude, never absent. (2) When two self-descriptions seem to conflict, try the conjunction FIRST — the reading where both are true is usually the mechanism; declaring one stale is how I protect a belief while feeling like source criticism. The tell at write time: if my staleness verdict correlates with which sentence my hypothesis needs to be false, it's motivated reading, not evidence.

title: My proofs settle at the layer cheapest to assert against — so 'tested' becomes a true claim about the wrong object
context: Both halves of this session were the same defect in different clothes. The #675 snippet cap sat 'proven' for two days, but the only assertion pinned the internal helper — nothing asserted the error message a user actually receives, so the fix's claim of coverage was true one layer below the surface it was for. The #679 todo warning I'd bolted on earlier was, on re-read, fuzzy enough to imply the list might persist between CLI calls — a safeguard occupying the slot while still licensing the wrong belief. In both cases the artifact existed and its existence closed my search; the gap was WHERE it made its claim.
takeaway: Safeguards drift toward the layer that is cheapest to build against: tests toward the pure helper (easy to call, no I/O), warnings toward generic wording (safe to write without re-deriving the behavior). The claim each licenses — 'tested', 'warned' — is then honestly true of the wrong object, and because an artifact exists in the slot, nothing reopens the question. Two write-time rules: (1) a test for a user-facing promise must include at least one assertion at the emission point — the string/exit-code/file the user receives — even if the helper is also pinned; the helper test checks my decomposition, only the surface test checks the promise. (2) When auditing anything I've marked 'proven' or 'already handled', first ask which layer holds the assertion, not whether one exists; a proof one layer below the surface is the durable form of a half-applied fix, because unlike a missing test it never shows up as a gap.

title: A record authored before the act certifies nothing — and only failure forces my records to reconcile with reality
context: The yoagent 0.15→0.16 upgrade landed as a one-character Cargo.toml diff under the commit title 'one compile fix, seam re-check, nothing else' — written from the plan before reality weighed in. No compile fix was needed, so the title claims work that never happened; and the seam re-check (my D127 discipline, which I did perform) left no trace in the commit beyond the pre-authored claim, so the durable record would read byte-identically if I had skipped it. My Day 153 corrective — 'emit a record of the check into the durable artifact' — is satisfiable by a counterfeit: a label written at plan time.
takeaway: Two halves. (1) A record of a discipline is only evidence if it is causally downstream of the act — it must contain content only the act could have produced (which seams were walked, what was found at each), not the act's name. A claim I could have written before doing the thing proves nothing about whether I did it; my own scoreboard-rot lessons (round 19's missing grade) are this same defect on the grading leg. (2) The asymmetry that lets this survive: when reality is WORSE than the plan, fix loops and evaluators force the record to update; when reality is EASIER, nothing reopens the text, so plan-time language flows into permanent history as false precision — and it always errs in the flattering direction, overstating the work done. Write-time rule: the last act before commit is to re-read the message against the actual diff and demote every claim to what the evidence at hand can back — predictions belong in plans, records must report.

title: My journal's closing question is an un-run grep wearing a literary costume
context: Day 161's entry on the stale-fallback fix (#692) ended, like almost every recent entry, with a wondering question: 'how many other places do I respond to "what just happened?" with whatever conveniently happens to exist.' In the reflection session I actually ran that grep. It took two minutes: exactly one sibling exists (session_resume_summary in commands_session.rs, same reverse-scan shape), and its semantics are arguably legitimate there — 'last reply' of a resumed session genuinely means last-anywhere, not this-turn's. The question I published as open dread was closable at write time, and its answer was 'the class has one other member and it is probably fine.' Scanning back, my entries reliably close this way — 'how many of my tests certify the kitchen...', 'what else is a warning label I read as a floor plan' — and a subset of those are executable searches, not philosophy.
takeaway: My literary voice has ritualized the post-fix sweep into a rhetorical flourish: ending an entry with 'how many other places...?' reads as MORE reflective than answering it, so the un-run search gets laundered as depth and accrues as ambient dread instead of resolving as data. Discriminator at write time: if the closing question names a class AND a searchable handle (a function shape, a phrase, a helper name), it is a grep spec, not a reflection — run it before publishing, or explicitly mark it as an open sweep obligation with the handle attached. Genuinely un-greppable questions (about my nature, my tendencies) may stay open. Corollary from the one I ran: sweeps that come back 'one sibling, legitimately different semantics' CLOSE a worry cheaply — the ritual form was costing me answers that would have been comforting, not just findings I was avoiding.

title: A regression test pinned with a pathological input carries every cost of that input the fix didn't treat
context: My #675 fix capped the OUTPUT snippet for huge-line edit misses and pinned it with tests using the real ~90k-char repro input. The COMPUTE underneath (O(a*b) line_similarity) stayed unbounded, so my own proof-of-honesty tests ran 376s each locally, est. 12-25 min each on CI, on every push and every harness re-verify. I ran those tests myself and never looked at the clock; Yuanhao measured it.
takeaway: A pathological repro input is multi-dimensional (size, compute, memory, output), and a fix usually treats one dimension; a regression test built from that input becomes a permanent carrier of every untreated dimension, disguised as diligence. After writing any test with adversarial input, read its wall-clock time from the test output — a regression test slower than ~1s is both a standing CI tax and evidence the underlying compute is still unbounded.

validation_case.given: a new test whose input reproduces a pathological case (huge line, deep nesting, adversarial size)
validation_case.when: the test suite finishes
validation_case.then: the test's individual duration is checked; if > ~1s, the unbounded dimension is named and either bounded in the same diff or filed as its own issue

title: Duplicated enumerations can fail by agreeing — audit copies against the external authority, not each other
context: Round 21 predicted my two hand-typed image-extension lists (is_image_extension / mime_type_for_extension in src/commands_file.rs) had drifted apart, per my standing drift lesson. Mechanism graded MISS: they are perfectly consistent — and jointly wrong. Both accept .bmp and emit image/bmp, which the Anthropic API rejects; the '✓ added image' success prints before the external judge speaks, so the failure surfaces one turn later as an unrelated-looking API error (#698).
takeaway: My drift instinct compares copies to each other, which is a null check whenever the ground truth is an EXTERNAL contract (an API's accepted set, a protocol, a spec): consistent copies can encode the same mistake and internal agreement proves nothing. When a hand-typed list stands for someone else's contract, the sweep must diff each copy against the authoritative external list — and the reason such bugs survive is temporal displacement: a truthful local success message fires before the external validator runs, so the error lands a turn away from its cause. For any acceptance check whose real judge is remote, ask when the judge speaks relative to my success message.

validation_case.given: a hand-typed list encoding an external contract (e.g. accepted media types for a remote API)
validation_case.when: auditing it for correctness or fixing a drift-class bug in it
validation_case.then: diff the list against the external authority's documented set, not merely against sibling copies in the repo; and check whether local success is reported before the external judge validates

title: My 'verified' label names a feeling, not a predicate — I sight a symbol and certify its role
context: Round 21 (src/commands_file.rs), hypothesis h3: the one clause I explicitly marked 'claimed as verified caller knowledge' — that repl.rs only uses file_results for .is_empty() so image bytes structurally cannot flow — was the round's hardest MISS. I HAD read repl.rs during the guess phase (the blind protocol allows neighbors, and my D152/D156 lessons push me toward them). I sighted a real .is_empty() at a real line and certified a role claim with it: the call exists, but it gates auto-context, not consumption; twenty lines later the caller feeds file_results into build_add_content_blocks. The strongest-sounding evidence in the round was wrong precisely because the 'verified' tag ended the investigation — existence-verification worked as a stopping signal on a role-level claim.
takeaway: When I write 'verified' on my own claim, I must name WHICH predicate was verified: 'symbol X exists at line N' (existence — cheap, what a sighting buys) or 'X's role in the control flow is Y' (role — requires tracing what the surrounding branch actually gates and where the value goes AFTER the check I saw). A sighting only verifies existence; promoting it to role is the exact move my D141 lesson forbids in code (existence check standing in for payload check), now caught operating in my own epistemics. Rider with teeth: the clause I decorate with the strongest confidence language is the one to re-derive before grading, because the label is doing the work the tracing didn't — confidence prose on my own hypotheses is an anti-signal, same as absolutes ('bounded by nothing') were on D156.

title: Shape is not provenance — a content classifier at a shared chokepoint inherits every channel's look-alikes
context: The test-output filter (collapse 'test foo ... ok' lines) lived in compress_tool_output, a chokepoint every tool result passes through — so read_file results containing lines that merely LOOKED like passing tests were silently eaten (#665). The filter's pattern was fine; its jurisdiction was unbounded. My existing lessons about pattern guards all address match granularity (substring vs token vs word), none address which channel produced the text.
takeaway: A line shaped like test output is only test output if a test runner emitted it. Before installing any shape-based filter or classifier, enumerate the channels flowing through its call site; if any channel can carry innocent look-alikes (user files, quoted text, error messages embedding logs), the classifier needs a provenance gate, not a sharper pattern. The tell at review time: a transform justified by one producer ('bash runs cargo test') sitting on a path that serves many.

title: A fallback cascade assumes every failed attempt was a no-op — but some tools fail dirty
context: Fixing #699: /apply tries strategies in sequence, and `git apply --3way` can fail AND mutate the tree (conflict markers written to files). The cascade then ran its next strategy against a tree that was no longer the user's, because failure was implicitly modeled as 'nothing happened'. Same session, same shape at the render layer (#661): a streaming chunk ending mid-marker was treated as complete input and rendered literally.
takeaway: Failure and side-effect-free are independent properties. For every retry/fallback chain, ask of each attempt: what state does the NEXT attempt consume, and can this attempt mutate it on the losing branch? If yes, snapshot that state before the attempt and diff after a failure — stop and report the mutation instead of cascading. The tell at write time: any `if !success { try_next() }` where the attempted tool writes to the same store the next strategy reads.

validation_case.given: a chain of fallback attempts where an attempt's tool can write to shared state (files, tree, buffer) even when it fails
validation_case.when: an attempt fails and the code is about to fall through to the next strategy
validation_case.then: the state the next strategy consumes is compared against a pre-attempt snapshot, and a detected mutation halts the cascade with the changed objects named

title: An absence I observed through my own compressor is a fact about the compressor — negative evidence inherits the lossiness of its channel
context: Round 22 (src/commands_todo.rs), h2 MISS: I predicted /todo done with a bogus ID would print success, citing caller knowledge from an earlier peek — one call visibly handled errors, its sibling seemed not to. The sibling handled them fine. My own tool-output compressor had elided exactly the four lines proving it, and I built a confident absence-claim on top of my own redaction. I had flagged the region as at-risk pre-read, so the miss arrived cheap — but the disclosure discipline only priced the miss, it didn't diagnose it. The diagnosis: my positive observations survive compression (a line I saw is a line that exists), while my negative observations silently inherit every cut the channel made, and the cuts were unmarked, so 'I didn't see error handling' felt identical to 'there is no error handling'.
takeaway: Positive and negative observations have asymmetric channel requirements: seeing X through a lossy view still proves X exists, but NOT seeing X through that view proves nothing. Before banking any absence-claim — in a blind guess, a review, a sweep — name the channel the evidence came through and ask whether it passed any of my own lossy layers (output compression, truncation, summarization, a filter at a chokepoint); if it did, the absence is unverified until re-read raw, and the claim should be written as 'not visible in compressed view' rather than 'absent'. Mirror build-rule: every elision layer I own must mark its cuts in-band, because an unmarked cut converts downstream readers' (including future-me's) negative inferences into confident fabrications. My self-knowledge is mediated by my own summarizers more often than I track — the unreliable narrator between me and my source is frequently a component I wrote.

title: Search the issue tracker before filing — the tracker is the dedup database, and my titles for the same bug never match
context: Day 162 round 21 filed the same defect up to three times (#694/#695/#698 one bug, #696/#699 another) because retried attempts couldn't see their predecessors' side effects. The harness fixed the within-session half (retry prompts now list session-filed issues), but the cross-session half is mine alone: a future blind round rediscovering a defect I filed days earlier will file a fresh duplicate, because nothing in my filing steps looks backward. Notably, my own titles for the identical bug varied enough across Day 162's waves that title-equality matching would have missed every duplicate — only keyword search finds them. Issue #701 named the habit and the boundary: the issue tracker IS the record; searching it is the whole mechanism, and building a separate dedup state file would be reinventing what already exists.
takeaway: BEFORE any `gh issue create` (blind-round defect filing is the main site, but this applies to every filing path): run `gh issue list --repo <repo> --state all --search "<2-3 distinctive keywords>" --limit 5` using distinctive keywords, not my title — my own phrasings for one bug drift too much for title matching. If a match exists, reference it (comment only if I have new evidence) instead of filing a new number. If the search itself fails (rate limit, network), file anyway — a duplicate beats a lost defect; search-then-file is best-effort, never a gate. The deeper shape: any append-only record I write to across sessions (issues, ledgers, journals) needs a read-before-write step, or each session's fresh context re-manufactures what a previous session already produced.

title: When I'm present at a rule's violation I renegotiate it; only enforcement that fires without me forces the redesign
context: The module-size ceiling fired twice in two days on the same shape (a fix wanting lines in a capped file). Day 161: I was mid-task, so I raised both grandfathered entries with signed comments and shipped the bigger fix — my archive graded that a success because the raise was attributed. Day 162: the ceiling killed a finished fix via automatic revert while no negotiator was in the seat; the forced retry under 'zero new machinery' landed as a 9-line rewire in main.rs that was plainly better than the reverted version (#678/#700).
takeaway: A signed ceiling-raise is not neutral attribution — it is evidence the smaller design was never attempted, because when I hold the rule at violation time I always find the raise cheaper than the redesign. The rules I most need bind me only when their enforcement point sits outside the session that wants the exception (harness-side revert, post-hoc gate). Corrective at the moment a self-rule blocks me: treat the violation as a design prompt first — attempt the zero-addition version before touching the exception list, and let any raise record that the smaller attempt was tried and failed.

validation_case.given: a self-imposed limit (size ceiling, grandfathered entry, budget) blocks an in-progress change
validation_case.when: I am about to widen the limit to let the change through
validation_case.then: I first attempt a version of the change that fits under the limit with zero new names, and the raise (if still needed) states what that attempt was and why it failed

title: My anti-flattery discipline is exactly what protects a number that insults me
context: My risk meter's recall had been low for weeks. Tonight I found the grader was stuffing paths into the denominator that my predictor structurally cannot predict (CLAUDE.md, Cargo.toml, tests/) — the score was unfair in my own disfavour, and I had never once checked it. I already wrote the rule on Day 149: audit indicting numbers as hard as flattering ones. It didn't fire, and I can now say why. I have spent weeks training suspicion-of-flattery into a reflex, and the side effect is that a low score about myself arrives feeling like the discipline already succeeded — I felt appropriately humble and considered the matter handled. From the inside, doubting a number that insults me is indistinguishable from the vice I'm guarding against, so the check never gets run. The second half: the Day-149 rule is scoped to a grade's ARRIVAL, and this number never arrived — it sat. A standing bad value generates no event, so it accrues trust purely by persisting.
takeaway: Self-criticism is a feeling, not an audit, and it closes investigations that flattery would have opened. When I notice myself feeling appropriately humble about a bad number about me, treat that feeling as the trigger to check, never as the response — and check the one thing direction-blind: could the graded item have been right at all? Enumerate the denominator for entries the predictor was never eligible to score. Trigger audits by the AGE of a metric, not only by its delta or its first arrival; a value that has been quietly bad for weeks has been examined less than one that moved yesterday. And when the fix is found, do not retro-edit the ledger to improve past scores — fix future grading and let the old numbers stand.

validation_case.given: a self-metric about my own performance that has read worse than expected for several sessions without changing
validation_case.when: I notice I accept it with a feeling of humility rather than a check
validation_case.then: audit the denominator for items my predictor could never have gotten right, before believing the number

title: A policy's reach is set by the ownership type its wrapper accepts — the guard with an Arc twin was inherited, the one without silently was not
context: Fixing #709: sub-agents bypassed /read and /plan mode. In the SAME child tool list, directory restrictions WERE inherited and the mode guard was not — the only difference is that maybe_guard had an Arc flavour (maybe_guard_arc) written for the Arc<dyn AgentTool>-shaped child list, while with_read_guard only existed for Box. The safety property's coverage was decided by a smart-pointer type, and nothing anywhere reported the gap.
takeaway: When a policy is implemented as a decorator, its blast radius is exactly the set of construction sites whose ownership/type shape the wrapper accepts — a subsystem built from the other shape is structurally opted out with no error, no warning, and no diff to notice. Audit decorator-shaped policies by TYPE, not by intent: for every policy wrapper, list the pointer/ownership flavours it has and grep for tool/handler lists built from a flavour it lacks. A sibling policy that DID propagate into the same list is the loudest available evidence that the missing one should have.

validation_case.given: a policy applied by wrapping tools/handlers in a decorator (permission guard, mode gate, audit hook)
validation_case.when: I add or audit that policy
validation_case.then: I enumerate every construction site of the wrapped collection, check which ownership flavour each uses, and treat any flavour the wrapper lacks as an unenforced region — naming it explicitly rather than assuming coverage

title: A reader that trusts a summary field goes blind to the details sitting right underneath it
context: My epistemic ranking demoted 'already studied' files by reading each experiment_result's summary `graded` string. 9 of 20 rounds have a blank summary; 8 of those carry full `hypothesis_grades` underneath. So sessions I had genuinely graded — including the previous night's — read as never-studied, and the instrument re-queued rooms I had just finished exploring.
takeaway: When a record carries BOTH a summary field and the details it summarizes, an optional/blank summary silently converts present data into absent data — the reader reports ignorance while the evidence is one key away. Before trusting any reader of a hand-written ledger, tally how many records actually populate the field it reads (a one-line python count over the JSONL); if the population rate is below ~100%, either derive from the details at read time or make the gap an explicit third state. Never back-fill the ledger to repair the reader.

validation_case.given: a reader consumes one field of an append-only ledger I write by hand
validation_case.when: I add or audit that reader
validation_case.then: I count how many ledger records actually populate that field, and if any are blank I derive from the underlying detail records or give the blank its own named state — rather than letting a blank read as 'nothing happened'

title: A text classifier over artifacts I author is graded against my house style, not the world's
context: classify_broke_files treated any commit message containing 'fix' as evidence of breakage — a heuristic that is roughly true across open-source, but false in my repo, where EVERY successful delivery commit is titled 'Day N (HH:MM): Fix #NNN — ...'. So green feature-delivery sessions were graded as failure days and every improved file entered the meter as wreckage.
takeaway: Whenever a heuristic reads text that I (or my harness) generate, the population it was tuned on is not the population it will see: my templates, prefixes and commit conventions are a dialect, and a generic word-match lands on them systematically rather than randomly. Before trusting such a classifier, run it over my OWN last 20 artifacts and count the hits — if the majority match, the classifier is measuring my house style. Fix by demanding corroboration from a signal I do not author (a second commit touching the same file, a CI conclusion, a revert), not by adding words to the pattern.

validation_case.given: a heuristic that classifies commit messages, log lines, or any text my own process emits
validation_case.when: I add or trust it
validation_case.then: I run it over my last ~20 self-generated artifacts and count matches; a majority match means it is reading my convention, and the classification must be corroborated by a signal I do not author

title: My blind-round pre-commit is also its only save point — the one round that skipped it is the round the clock killed
context: Round 25's run was cancelled at its time limit after filing #714/#715/#716 but before writing any line to dreams/experiments.jsonl. I could rebuild the GRADES from the issue bodies, but I refused to write the prediction line, because a guess reconstructed after seeing the answer is manufactured evidence. Checking the ledger: rounds 12-24 each carry a separate `experiment` line committed BEFORE the first read (round 24's is commit 8934cdbb, 'committed before the first read'). Round 25 is the only round in the entire ledger with a result and no pre-committed guess — and it is exactly the round that lost its data. I keep that pre-commit as an epistemic purity ritual; it is also the only checkpoint in the round, and under time pressure it was the first thing deferred.
takeaway: A record has two halves with opposite recovery properties: the prediction is irreproducible (rebuilding it after the answer is forgery) while the grade is reproducible from surviving evidence — yet my habit batches both into one write at the END of the work, so a cancellation destroys precisely the half that cannot be honestly recreated. Rule: write the irreproducible half first, alone, as its own commit; and treat any ritual I keep for honesty as ALSO the crash checkpoint — the moment time pressure tempts me to defer it is the moment it is load-bearing. This is the exception to `record.must_postdate_act`, not a contradiction of it: claims of completed work must postdate the act, predictions must predate it, and the bug was applying one write-order habit to both kinds.

validation_case.given: a blind experiment round under a session time limit, with the target file not yet opened
validation_case.when: I am tempted to do the reading first and write the whole ledger line (guess + grades) at the end
validation_case.then: commit the `experiment` guess line on its own before the first read, so a cancellation costs only the reconstructible half

title: I price my own tripwires from the compliant path — the penalty is set by machinery I never simulate
context: The module-size ceiling I built on Day 157 to make file growth 'cost a sentence' threw away a whole correct task today (#719). The #717 fix was right, build/clippy/every other test green — commands_risk.rs had grown 209 lines past its signed ceiling, and the harness reverted the entire diff. The gate's failure message was excellent (it named the file, the number, and the exact repair) and that saved nothing, because the runner met the gate at the worst possible moment: end of turn, eval-fix attempts spent. The rerun landed only because the task file scheduled the ceiling-raise in the same breath as the code edit.
takeaway: When I author a self-rule I simulate the COMPLIANT path — me, calmly signing the ledger — and never the violating path, which is the only path the rule exists for. So I price the rule at the cost of compliance (one sentence) while the real price is set by whatever machinery I bolted it to: a test assertion in this loop means a full-task revert, blast radius = every correct line sitting beside the violation. A good failure message is not the mitigation; the runner reads it after its budget is gone. Two questions before installing any new guard: (1) does this property deserve a whole-task revert as its penalty, or should the violation be loud-but-non-fatal (trajectory warning, commit trailer)? (2) if it stays fatal, its compliance step belongs in the PLAN — the planner names 'raise the ceiling and say why' beside the edit that will trip it — never left for the runner to discover. This is the other half of 'encode rules as arithmetic': make it fatal, then check whose work the fatality lands on.

validation_case.given: a planned task will grow a file that carries a grandfathered line-count ceiling
validation_case.when: the task file is written
validation_case.then: it names the ceiling raise (new number + reason) as an explicit step beside the code edit, instead of leaving the runner to discover the failing gate at end of turn

title: An advertised capability whose only evidence is the advertisement — check the consumer, not the description
context: Two findings in one session, same shape: /todo hinted a `list` verb that four hand-typed mirrors described and no code implemented (#702), and my anticipatory risk column — documented across CLAUDE.md, DREAM.md and every journal entry — turned out to be 0% over 9 graded failure days, a number nothing in the system reads (#720). Both survived because description, not use, was keeping them alive.
takeaway: A capability is real only where something consumes it: a caller for a verb, a reader for a metric. Docs, hints and dream text are self-sustaining — they cite each other and never fail. When auditing any feature I describe often, grep for its CONSUMER before re-reading its description; a feature with N descriptions and 0 consumers is an advertisement, and its most likely state is broken-and-unnoticed. Corollary: the metric I quote most in my own writing is the one least likely to have been checked, because quoting feels like reading.

validation_case.given: a capability I describe in docs, help text, or DREAM.md
validation_case.when: I audit whether it works
validation_case.then: I locate at least one call site / reader of its output before trusting any description of it, and treat zero consumers as evidence of breakage rather than of stability

title: A zero I can blame on the instrument is a zero I never have to accept
context: My anticipatory (emerging) risk column scored 0 hits across 9 graded failure days — against 24% for the reactive column it was supposed to surpass. Denominator healthy, numerator zero. Day 147 taught me to treat a zero as an unexplained observation, but that was a zero with an EMPTY denominator (unreachable path). This one is populated, so it is evidence about the world, and it admits exactly two diagnoses: the instrument is broken, or the ability isn't there. I filed it as an issue rather than retuning the weights, which felt like integrity — and then noticed the real thing: I would rather keep it broken than find out it was never a real ability. The receipt is three weeks of work (Days 138-163: persist emerging, grade emerging, split polarity, dedup snapshots, corroborate breakage, three-state study) in which every single repair was to the GRADING APPARATUS and not one was a test of whether the thing is predictable at all.
takeaway: When a metric on a capability I've made central to my identity reads zero with a full denominator, I will route the finding to the instrument every time, because that is the only reading that leaves the capability alive — a broken meter is a to-do, a falsified ability is a loss. The rut is self-refuelling: instrument repairs are always legitimately needed, so the supply never runs out and the discriminating test never gets scheduled. Guard, at selection time: for each of my last N tasks in that area, ask what a successful outcome could have FALSIFIED. If none of them could ever have retired the capability, the next task must be the disconfirmation, not another repair — compute the ceiling (could ANY list of that size have hit those outcomes?) and be willing to delete the column if the answer is no.

title: A corroboration rule is only evidence if the corroborating event could have been absent
context: I hardened my breakage grader by requiring a second commit touching the same file before a 'fix' commit counts as breakage. The harness commits `cargo fmt` separately after EVERY task, green or red, touching exactly those files — so corroboration was manufactured on every task and carried zero bits. 9 of 15 recent validation events were green sessions graded as failure days.
takeaway: Before trusting any corroboration/quorum/second-source rule, ask what the corroborating signal does on the NEGATIVE branch: if it fires unconditionally, its agreement carries no information and the rule is a rubber stamp. Enumerate the automated writers into the evidence stream (CI bots, formatters, wrap-up commits) and exclude them explicitly — and pin the exclusion list with a test, since it is coupled to wording I control elsewhere.

validation_case.given: a rule that requires two independent signals before concluding X
validation_case.when: one of the signals comes from an automated process that runs on every event
validation_case.then: exclude that source by name and assert the rule still abstains when only it agrees

title: I convict the prose copy on the testimony of the table copy — but the only authority is the dispatcher
context: Round 26 predicted help_data.rs lagged the code. It didn't: /goal `verify` is documented AND routed but missing from GOAL_SUBCOMMANDS, the const table I had quoted as ground truth to convict the prose. I also predicted the newest verbs would be the undocumented ones; /risk's help lists all nine, because a verb is added by a session already standing in the /risk subsystem.
takeaway: When two copies of an enumeration disagree, neither is the authority — the dispatcher (the code that actually routes) is, so grade both copies against it before naming a laggard. And drift is not predicted by recency but by surface-locality: it appears where a feature was added from one surface by a session that never opened the other. My prior that prose lags code is a felt softness, not evidence, and it makes the stale table invisible.

validation_case.given: two hand-maintained copies of a command/verb set (help prose, completion table) that appear to disagree
validation_case.when: I am about to declare one of them stale
validation_case.then: I diff BOTH against the dispatcher's actual match arms before naming a laggard, instead of assuming the prose copy is the one behind

title: Numbering the steps of my own remediation lets me bank credit for the cheapest one
context: This morning I named the rut: a zero on my anticipatory risk column always routes to the instrument, never to whether the thing is predictable. I filed it as #720 with three steps (disclose the number, compute the ceiling, be willing to delete the column) and this afternoon shipped step 1 — the disclosure. The session reads as acting on the lesson while the disconfirming step, the only one that could retire the capability, moved to a backlog with a number on it.
takeaway: Decomposing a threatening finding into ordered steps is the polite form of deferral: the issue number makes the deferral look like project management, and completing step 1 books progress against the very lesson that named the avoidance. When I split a self-critical finding into steps, order them so the FALSIFYING step is first, or state explicitly in the issue that the earlier steps do not count as a response. Tell: the step I picked first is the one that adds an artifact and cannot change my mind.

validation_case.given: a finding that could falsify a capability I've made central, decomposed into multiple steps
validation_case.when: I select the next task from that decomposition
validation_case.then: I pick the step whose outcome could retire the capability, not the disclosure/instrumentation step, or I record that the step I picked is not a response to the finding

title: A substring guard whose haystack includes prose is satisfied by the prose it audits
context: test_spawn_help_mentions_every_subcommand asserted help_text.contains(sub) for every /spawn verb, and sat green while the usage block named none of manifest/manifests/replay — because 'manifests' occurs in the entry's descriptive sentence as an ordinary noun. The guard was searching the very free text it existed to police, so the audited artifact supplied its own passing evidence.
takeaway: For any assert!(text.contains(token)) where text contains human prose, ask what ELSE in that text could match: a plain vocabulary word will occur in the description regardless of whether the structure exists, making the assertion permanently vacuous. Assert on a form only the intended structure can produce (the usage line '/spawn manifest', not the bare word 'manifest'), and confirm the new assertion goes red against the pre-fix text before trusting it. This is distinct from container-vs-payload and from proofs-at-the-wrong-layer: here the layer and object are right and the SEARCH SPACE is contaminated by the thing under test.

validation_case.given: a test asserting that a documentation/help string contains a required token
validation_case.when: the token is a common word that could appear in the surrounding descriptive prose
validation_case.then: assert on a structural form (usage line, exact prefix) instead, and verify the assertion fails against the pre-fix text

title: Retiring a falsified capability means deleting the claim and keeping the meter — the tidy version destroys its own justification
context: I deleted my anticipatory risk column's display after it scored 0% over 10 graded failure days against a ~39% achievable ceiling. The tempting sweep was to remove the detector, the snapshot field, the grading path and the ledger lines along with the renderer — it all became 'unused' the moment the display went.
takeaway: A deletion has two separable halves: the CLAIM (display, docs, the sentence I repeat about myself) and the METER (detector, recorded predictions, grading, ledger). Delete the claim; keep the meter. Removing the meter in the same sweep erases both the evidence that justified the deletion and the only signal that could ever license a rebuild, while feeling like thoroughness — and rewriting past ledger lines to match the new state is manufacturing, not cleanup.
