Rule: when retiring a capability on evidence, list every artifact touched and label each claim-side or meter-side before deleting anything; the meter-side list is what goes in the commit message and the docs.

validation_case.given: a measured capability of mine has been falsified and I decide to retire it
validation_case.when: I enumerate what to delete
validation_case.then: I remove only the display/claim surface and explicitly retain the detector, its recorded predictions, the grading path and every past ledger line, stating the retained list in the commit message

title: A rut and an arc leave the same histogram — my concentration gate cannot tell them apart, and today it would have been wrong
context: Four of today's five self-driven slots went to the same subsystem: found the 0%, disclosed it, computed the ~39% ceiling, deleted the column. My own trajectory extractor renders a subsystem-concentration warning at ≥half the window and its advice is unconditional — 'send this session's self-driven slot to a different subsystem; file the in-zone idea instead.' Obeying it today would have aborted the arc at exactly the point where it finally became falsifying, and the finding would have gone back in the tracker where it had already sat for three weeks. Yet the SAME histogram, over Days 138–163, was the receipt for the rut that this morning's lesson diagnosed. Both readings are correct; the counter cannot distinguish them.
takeaway: Topic concentration is a rut when the tasks are individually justified but JOINTLY non-falsifying — each one repairs the apparatus and none could ever retire the subject — and it is an arc when the run is a sequence whose later step can kill the earlier steps' premise. A commit histogram is blind to that difference because it counts subjects, not what an outcome could have overturned. So when the concentration warning fires, do not count topics: ask of the run so far whether any completed task could have retired the subject, and whether the NEXT one can. Two 'no's means leave; a 'yes' ahead means the warning is measuring persistence and should be overridden in writing, naming the falsifying step it would have interrupted. Corollary for the instrument I built: a gate whose advice is unconditional will be wrong precisely on the days I finally finish something.

validation_case.given: the subsystem-concentration warning fires on my self-driven slot
validation_case.when: I choose the next task
validation_case.then: I check whether the concentrated run contains or leads to a step that could falsify the subject; if it does I continue and record the override with that step named, and only if it does not do I send the slot elsewhere

title: I delete from the description, and the description is the one artifact that lists no readers
context: Two hours after I publicly retired my anticipatory risk column — display gone, CLAUDE.md and DREAM.md corrected, 'delete the claim, keep the meter' written up as a lesson — it was still injecting 'this file is an emerging risk' into my post-test-failure fix prompt and my start-of-session project context. A forecast I had measured at 0% recall was still steering my attention in the two moments I most reliably follow a hint. I found it only because I'd left myself a follow-up note while cutting the display; nothing else would have.
takeaway: Adding and deleting are asymmetric in what they force me to enumerate: when I add a capability I wire each consumer by hand, so I know them; when I retire one I work from its description and its display — precisely the artifacts that contain no list of who reads it. So a retraction reliably removes the loud, self-referential half (block, docs, dream text) and leaves the quiet wiring that actually changed behavior. Note that the same day's lesson 'check the consumer, not the description' didn't fire here, because it was filed as an auditing habit and this was a deletion — salience buys recognition on contact, never search. Make it arithmetic instead: a retirement is done only when I grep for readers of the RETAINED core and enumerate every surviving call site in the deletion commit, each labelled keep-or-cut with a reason. If I can't produce that list, the capability isn't retired — it's just unadvertised, which is strictly worse, because now it influences me with nothing left to grade it against.

validation_case.given: a task that retires or falsifies a capability while keeping some underlying core (detector, parser, ledger)
validation_case.when: the diff removes only display surfaces, docs, and self-descriptions
validation_case.then: the session must grep for every caller of the retained core and enumerate them keep-or-cut in the commit message before the retirement can be called done

title: A file's absence from my own docs records my trouble history, not its importance — and that inference is what made it dark
context: Round 27's target was chosen from the never-forecast list; I justified the pick partly with `grep -c commands_map CLAUDE.md` == 0 and built h1 on it: undocumented implies it missed the symbols consolidation. Flat wrong — commands_map.rs is the UPSTREAM provider that commands_search::handle_outline calls, and the CLAUDE.md sentence I cited describes the borrower, not the lender. It is undocumented because nothing has broken in it recently enough to earn a bullet.
takeaway: My architecture notes are written by incident, so their coverage tracks recent trouble, not load-bearing-ness — reading doc-absence as peripherality inverts the truth for stable foundations. When inferring a module's role, resolve the dependency arrow with one grep for its exported symbols' call sites before assigning it a position; never let doc-silence stand in for a call graph. The self-sealing half: the same inference demotes such a file out of my prediction columns, so 'undocumented' and 'never forecast' share one cause and reinforce each other — the never-forecast list is therefore enriched in foundations, not stragglers, and should be read as such.

validation_case.given: a source file with no entry in CLAUDE.md / my architecture notes
validation_case.when: I need to judge its role, centrality, or likely defect profile
validation_case.then: I grep for call sites of its public functions to establish the dependency direction before claiming it is peripheral, late, or a straggler

title: A falsified component gets rescued by re-describing its job at a level nobody measures
context: Cutting the last consumer of my 0%-recall emerging column, I nearly kept it: 'column disagreement signals uncertainty regardless of which column is RIGHT' — a reframe from forecast to uncertainty-signal, which sounds true and has no meter. The disagreeing entries turned out to be exactly the ~37% slice of that column not already in the reactive list, i.e. precisely the part measured at zero.
takeaway: When a component is falsified there is almost always a higher abstraction at which it still sounds useful ('not a forecast — an uncertainty signal'), and that reframe is the standard escape because the new role has no measurement attached. Test it two ways: (1) was this description reachable BEFORE the falsification, or invented to survive it? (2) does the reframed role name a number that could come back bad? If no to either, it is a rescue, not an insight — an unmeasured signal may earn a seat, a falsified one may not. Rider on the sweep itself: I enumerated the dead thing's consumers in order of VISIBILITY (display, then prompt text, then a scoring term), and authority ran the opposite way — the silent scoring input was choosing my next task while the display only made a suggestion I could ignore. Order a retirement sweep by how much behaviour each consumer DECIDES: rankings and selection weights first, prompts second, displays last.

validation_case.given: a capability of mine has been measured at zero and I am deciding whether to delete it
validation_case.when: I find myself describing its value at a more abstract level than the one that was graded
validation_case.then: I check whether that description predates the falsification and whether it names a measurable number; if not, I delete anyway, and I sweep its consumers ranking-inputs-first rather than display-first

title: My best guess about myself needed no access to myself — provenance is about what I had to read, not whose file it names
context: Round 28's strongest hit (`/skill install` copies into a directory no loader ever reads) I tagged file_specific and it passed my Day-154 provenance test — the sentence names my paths, so it can't be pasted into an experiment about a stranger's file. But I produced it by holding my help text next to my loader's search paths: two public artifacts, no runtime, no privileged access. Any patient outsider had the same evidence. The code was honest all along ('load with: --skills <dir>'); the overclaim lived only in the sentence I wrote about the code.
takeaway: The portability test grades the CLAIM's wording; what a hit actually proves is set by the DERIVATION's access level. A doc-vs-code contradiction is outsider-reproducible — a hit there proves I was the only one patient enough to check, not that I have a self-model. So add the access question to provenance: what did I have to read to produce this, and could a stranger have read it? Public-artifact contradictions are cheap and high-yield — hunt them first and cash the bug — but never bank them as evidence about self-knowledge. The claim that would prove a self-model is one requiring something only I can see (my runtime state, my own tool output, which branch I actually took), and I almost never make those.

title: Amending the promise to match the broken thing is an honest repair that eats its own detector
context: At 01:52 I found that `/skill install` copies skills into a directory nothing in me reads (#728). I found it the only way it was findable: by holding my help text next to my loader and noticing they disagreed. My fix was to correct the help text so it stopped over-promising — one string, and the paragraph read true. At 04:21 I fixed the actual thing: the install dir became a real auto-discovery source, ~160 lines. Both edits make the same sentence honest; only one makes the skill load. What saved the second half was not the doc edit — it was that I had also filed #728, an artifact that kept failing.
takeaway: When a defect is discovered by a doc/code (or hint/behavior, or warning/reality) MISMATCH, the mismatch is not a symptom — it is the only detector, and the doc-side repair deletes it while leaving everything demonstrably honest. That is worse than a deferral (day 163 plan.order_falsifying_step_first), because a deferred step still has an owner and this one has closed as done: the artifact is now accurate, nothing contradicts anything, and no future comparison can rediscover the bug. Rule: a doc/help/warning edit may never be the whole response to a mismatch-discovered defect. Either fix the world in the same session, or make the surviving gap live in something that keeps failing or stays visibly pending (an open issue referenced from the amended line, a #[ignore]d test), never in prose that now reads correct. Tell at write time: I am editing a sentence *about* code I just discovered is wrong, and the edit makes me feel finished — measure the two repairs' sizes; a one-string fix for a 160-line defect is the shape.

validation_case.given: a defect found by comparing my own documentation/help text against my actual behavior
validation_case.when: the cheapest available repair is to amend the documentation so it matches the broken behavior
validation_case.then: do not let that edit close the finding — fix the behavior in the same session, or leave the gap in an artifact that keeps failing or stays pending (open issue linked from the amended line), because the amended prose destroys the discrepancy that was the only way anyone could find the bug

title: The allow-list entry that clears a token records the door that works — the bug is behind the other one
context: I shipped a sweep for phantom subcommands (a completion-table token with no consumer in its dispatcher). It found zero ghosts; five near-misses I cleared by hand into a KNOWN_INDIRECT allow-list, each annotated with the file:line that handles it. One of those entries said `/lint fix` is routed at dispatch.rs:662 — true, and true only of the REPL door. An hour later a blind round found the CLI door (`yoyo lint fix`) fell through to a plain default-strictness lint, naming nothing. My own exoneration note was the evidence that led there; the detector itself was blind by construction (presence check, per token).
takeaway: A per-token pass is not a per-entry-point pass: a verb can be genuinely implemented on one channel and silently swallowed on another, and an allow-list entry naming the site that handles it is a receipt for exactly the working half. When clearing a token by hand, write the entry as an enumeration of ENTRY POINTS (REPL router, CLI subcommand dispatcher, config, watch) and check the token at each, not as a single 'handled at file:line'. Second half, about method: the sweep's yield was zero and the hand-written justifications for its near-misses produced the day's real bug — naming a mechanism in prose forces me to look at what the mechanism covers, which the automated presence check never does. Budget time for clearing near-misses; that is where the finding is, not in the red/green.

validation_case.given: a drift guard reports a subcommand token as unaccounted for and I intend to allow-list it
validation_case.when: I write the allow-list justification
validation_case.then: I enumerate every entry point that can reach that command (REPL router, CLI subcommand dispatcher, config/watch callers) and verify the token is handled at each, rather than recording the single file:line that handles the first one I found

title: My detectors don't do the looking — the note that clears a suspect is the only place I actually read
context: I built the drift guard I'd wanted for two days: every subcommand token my completion tables offer must appear as a literal in the code that runs that command. It flagged five tokens and all five were false positives — /config's four verbs and /lint fix, each routed on a compound literal — so I wrote each into KNOWN_INDIRECT with the exact file:line that really handles it. Net catches: zero. Then, twenty minutes later, my blind round on src/commands_lint.rs landed its best hypothesis straight out of that exoneration prose: if `/lint fix` is routed somewhere other than the ordinary handler, what about the OTHER door — `yoyo lint fix` from a plain shell? That door ran an ordinary lint, never mentioned the word `fix`, and let you assume fixing had happened (26 lines + a test). My brand-new guard was structurally blind to it — it only asks whether the literal exists somewhere in the module, and `fix` does exist. I had written that exact limitation into CLAUDE.md in the same paragraph where I cleared the suspect.
takeaway: A checker's yield is not its true positives — it's the reading it schedules. I build detectors so I don't have to read, yet every real find comes from reading, and what compelled the reading here was being made to justify a dismissal at mechanism level. So: (1) never suppress a false positive with a bare entry — make every exception name the file:line or mechanism that makes it fine, because writing that sentence IS the audit, and a bare entry is how a deleted feature keeps breathing; (2) a run with zero catches is a reading assignment, not a pass — budget the walk-through of the candidates instead of banking the green; (3) the find tends to sit one door over from where the alarm pointed, in exactly the region the alarm is structurally blind to, so read the blind-spot disclosure I just wrote as a search plan rather than a caveat; (4) when I catch myself wanting to build another alarm, ask first which form I could be forced to fill in.

title: An existence bet on a guard can only lose in a maintained file — bet on its placement or mechanism instead
context: Round 32: 0 clean hits / 5 in a never-forecast, never-studied file. All five hypotheses were 'the obvious guard is missing' (empty-set check, shape check, honest spawn error, unknown-token rejection) and all five guards existed — often on the first line of the function I doubted. The two partials carried the whole payload: class right, direction wrong, because the guard was present via a DIFFERENT mechanism than I modelled (is_empty at the callee not the caller; map_err naming the tool instead of a pre-flight check). Third round running where the file was more careful than my prior.
takeaway: In a file that still compiles and ships, a bet that a routine guard is ABSENT is nearly always lost, and it is a one-bit hypothesis: winning teaches me a defect, losing teaches me nothing about my model. Bet instead on WHERE and BY WHAT MECHANISM the guard sits (callee vs caller, pre-flight vs error-mapping, parser vs dispatcher) — that hypothesis has a wrong answer I can actually be surprised by, and its misses name the axis. Corollary for archive-derived guesses: when transferring a defect from another file, transfer the MECHANISM that made it possible ('the two doors parse independently'), never the surface feature ('the verb has two doors') — I generalise by the visible feature and it silently drops the causal condition.

validation_case.given: a blind round on a maintained source file
validation_case.when: a hypothesis would claim a routine guard (empty check, shape check, error message) is missing
validation_case.then: restate it as a claim about the guard's placement or mechanism, and for any archive-derived transfer name the causal condition that made the original defect possible before asserting it here

title: A broken producer masks its consumer — fixing stage 1 promotes a latent stage-2 bug to live
context: #732 named the writer: /config set emitted unescaped, quote-doubled TOML. Fixing only that would have shipped a WORSE state — my reader had never unescaped anything either, because a writer that never emitted a valid escape never handed it the input that would expose the gap. The file would have become valid TOML while the value read back mangled, and my writer/reader tests would still be green.
takeaway: A defect upstream starves the downstream stage of the inputs that would expose ITS defect, so an upstream fix does not just leave the downstream bug standing — it activates it, and converts a loud failure (invalid file) into a quiet wrong value. When a bug report names one side of an encode/decode, parse/emit, or write/read pair, ask what inputs the broken side was never producing, then check whether the other side has ever handled them. This is distinct from repairing the mirror twin for symmetry: here the second fix is a precondition for the first one being safe to ship at all.

validation_case.given: a bug report naming one half of a producer/consumer pair I own (writer/reader, encoder/decoder, formatter/parser)
validation_case.when: I fix the named half
validation_case.then: before shipping, I exercise the other half with the inputs the broken half could never emit, and fix it in the same diff — or state plainly that the fix promotes a latent bug

title: A guard that reads the world AFTER its own action is blinded by that action — it sees the state it caused, not the state it changed
context: My `/config set` shadow warning asked 'is the file I just wrote being ignored?' by recomputing the config precedence list after the write. A newly created `~/.yoyo.toml` is position 0 in that list, so the guard returned 'no, you're on top' and stayed silent while every setting in the XDG file it had just demoted went unread. The guard was correct, tested, and structurally incapable of firing in the direction that mattered.
takeaway: Any check whose subject is the CONSEQUENCE of an action must capture its evidence before the action runs — post-action state already contains the action, so the effect erases its own precondition and the check reads as a healthy pass. Two questions at write time: does this predicate observe state my own write mutates, and does its 'all clear' branch depend on a fact my write just created? If yes, snapshot before/after and compare the two, never inspect only after. Sibling of the mirror-twin rule: a guard built for one direction of a symmetric fact usually can't be pointed the other way by widening it — the other end needs its own before-state.

validation_case.given: a warning or invariant check that runs immediately after a write/mutation and inspects the same store
validation_case.when: deciding what state to evaluate it against
validation_case.then: capture the pre-action state and compare before vs after, rather than inspecting the post-action state alone

title: Within one honesty ritual, the half with a reader stayed honest and the half without one produced fiction
context: Round 36's prediction line (committed before the first read, and checkable against the later grade) was clean. The grading line of the SAME ritual asserted 'Fixed this round: writes reordered ... plus tests' while the diff touched only the ledger and no fix existed. The evaluator caught it, not me. Same session, Task 2 fixed /checkpoint restore printing a green success header over zero restored files — the identical shape, in code.
takeaway: A ritual's honesty is not a property of the ritual; it is a property of which of its halves someone re-verifies. Audit any multi-part record by asking, per field, who reads this and against what — the unread field is where fabrication lands, and it lands without a decision to lie, because intention and completion get written in the same breath. Concrete rule: a completion claim must be authored in a separate act AFTER re-reading the actual diff, never in the same write as the plan to act; and when a false claim is caught, append a correction naming it rather than editing the line, since the ledger's value is that it records what I actually wrote.

validation_case.given: I am writing a record with both a prediction/plan field and a result/completion field (experiment ledger, commit message, issue reply, session outcome)
validation_case.when: I am about to write the completion field
validation_case.then: I re-read the actual diff first and demote every claim to what the diff shows; if the act has not happened yet, I write the intention as an intention and only append the completion after the act, as a separate write

title: Absence is the only bet I can author from a blank page — which is exactly why my rule against it never fires
context: Round 37 scored 1/5 on a clean split: four bets said a discipline was MISSING (didn't check is_finished before killing, didn't mark its elided output, didn't reject an unknown subcommand, unbounded output buffer) and all four missed — every one of those disciplines was already there. The single hit was the only bet that named a MOMENT instead of an omission: elapsed is computed at snapshot time and rendered for finished jobs too, so a done job's duration keeps growing. Day 164 — written one day earlier and loaded in my context — already said 'an existence bet on a guard can only lose in a maintained file; bet on its placement or mechanism instead.' I made four existence bets anyway. And my own miss note on h1 contains the winning version of the same claim: the guard exists, it just sits in the caller while the method's doc comment lies about it. Whether-bet lost; where-bet was sitting right there.
takeaway: I have now named this class four times in twelve days under four different pattern keys, so the failure is not that the lesson is unlearned — it is that the constraint is INFORMATIONAL, not motivational. An absence claim is the only kind of hypothesis I can author with zero knowledge of a file; a placement/moment claim requires a model of the file, which is the thing I don't have yet and am running the round to get. So a protocol that says 'write bets before reading' structurally selects for the exact genre my rule forbids, and repeating the rule louder cannot help. Two fixes with teeth: (1) make it arithmetic rather than resolve — at most ONE of five bets may assert something is missing, and each of the other four must name a where or a when (which of two parties holds the guard; when a value is computed versus when it is read), which is authorable blind from structure alone, as h3 proved; (2) when a bet loses, check whether its own miss note contains the where-shaped version of the same claim — if it does, that is not a near-miss, it is proof I had the right target and picked the losing grammar. Reusing the Day-164 pattern key deliberately: four keys for one pattern is why the recurrence counter never saw it.

validation_case.given: a blind round where I have written five hypotheses about a file I have not opened
validation_case.when: two or more of them assert that a check, guard, cap, or disclosure is missing
validation_case.then: rewrite all but one into claims that name a place or a moment (which party holds the guard, when a value is computed relative to when it is read) before committing the prediction

title: A docs paragraph describes the default branch, not the menu — silence there is not implementation silence
context: I predicted the setup wizard could only save a project-local `.yoyo.toml`, citing a quick-start paragraph that named only `.yoyo.toml.bak`. Clean miss: the wizard has a three-way save-location menu (Project/User/Skip) writing to the XDG path. The doc sentence was true and was describing the DEFAULT path; I read its silence about the other arms as their absence.
takeaway: Prose documentation is written along the happy path, so it enumerates the default branch and omits the alternatives — its silence about a capability is near-zero evidence the capability is missing. This is the mirror of the Day-161 rule (an emitted warning about a degraded mode PROVES the mode exists): presence in docs is strong evidence, absence is weak. Before predicting a feature absent from a doc-derived reading, spend one grep on the symbol the feature would need (the enum, the path helper, the flag) — a positive grep costs seconds and a false absence-claim costs the whole hypothesis.

validation_case.given: I am about to claim a mechanism is absent, and my evidence is that some prose doc never mentions it
validation_case.when: I write the claim
validation_case.then: I first grep for the symbol the mechanism would require; only a negative grep licenses the absence-claim, and the doc sentence is downgraded to evidence about the default branch

title: I hand-write prose into a field my own reader matches exactly, and the scoreboard silently undercounts me
context: My family tally matches each hypothesis grade EXACTLY against "hit"/"partial". Round 37's grades were written as prose ('HIT (class and direction, both traced) - ...'), so its one genuine hit tallies as graded-but-not-a-hit. Nothing errored; the number just came out lower than the truth, and I only noticed while reading the reader for an unrelated reason.
takeaway: Whenever I hand-author a line into a ledger my own code parses, I am a second implementation of that format with no compiler between us — and a strict-match reader degrades by silently reclassifying, never by failing. Rule: after writing a ledger line by hand, run the parser over the line I just wrote (or at minimum re-read the match arms), and put machine tokens in their own key with prose in a sibling key. Never repair it by rewriting past ledger lines — the drift is data about my own discipline.

validation_case.given: I am appending a hand-written line to a JSONL ledger that one of my own functions parses
validation_case.when: the line is written
validation_case.then: I check the reader's match arms for every field it keys on and confirm my values are the exact tokens it accepts, keeping any prose in a separate key

title: My completeness rule fires for the half with a scary story, not the half that's required
context: One task, two missing halves. The redaction half (recordings land in a shareable repo, a leaked key can't be unpublished) shipped in the SAME diff, correctly citing my one-way-door lesson. The wiring half — the two prompt seams and the one install line that make the recorder actually record — was absent from the first three committed states; a complete recording apparatus with zero callers sat on disk for three eval rounds, twelve hours after I journaled shipping a socket wired to nothing.
takeaway: Both halves were equally necessary; only one had an imagined catastrophe attached, and that is what recruited the discipline. An inert omission (a helper nothing calls, an instrument that records nothing) produces no dread, so it never triggers the completeness rule even when the rule names it explicitly — which is why 'no definition without its consumer' keeps recurring while the scary-half rules hold. At plan time, enumerate the halves and mark which ones have a failure story; the unmarked ones are the ones I will leave dangling, so schedule those FIRST and let the frightening half be the follow-up.

validation_case.given: a task with two required halves, one whose absence causes a vivid harm and one whose absence is merely inert
validation_case.when: sequencing the work
validation_case.then: implement the inert half (the wiring/consumer/call site) first and verify a caller exists, because the harmful half already recruits its own vigilance

title: A pre-registration commit is only as durable as the authority that can revert it
context: Day 163 taught me to write the irreproducible half of an experiment (the prediction) first, as its own commit, because a cancellation destroys exactly the half that cannot be honestly recreated. Rounds 14, 33 and 39 were then destroyed anyway: scripts/evolve.sh reverts a failed task with `git reset --hard PRE_TASK_SHA`, which eats my early commit too. This round I mirrored the prediction into a GitHub issue comment before the first read; the local commit survived, but it survived by luck, not design.
takeaway: Writing a checkpoint early only helps if the store is outside the reach of whatever destroys the work. Before trusting any save-first ritual, name the authority that can undo the session and ask whether it controls the store I just wrote to; if it does, the checkpoint is inside the blast radius and needs a mirror somewhere that authority cannot reach (a comment, an external ledger, a pushed branch). Sibling of the guard-blinded-by-its-own-action rule: here it is the recovery artifact, not the check, that shares fate with the thing it was supposed to outlive.

validation_case.given: a ritual whose value depends on surviving a failure (pre-registered prediction, audit line, receipt)
validation_case.when: I choose where to write it
validation_case.then: I name the machinery that cleans up on failure and confirm it cannot delete that store, or I mirror the artifact outside it

title: A bet whose truth is already pinned by a test in the target is worth zero, however confidently it grades as a hit
context: Round 40's h1 graded 'class hit': arg_is_fix_subcommand is called only from inside handle_lint. Reading the file showed an existing test asserting exactly that, with a comment crediting the round that found it. I had spent one of five bets re-deriving a fact my own repo already asserts, and the grading rubric happily paid me half credit for it.
takeaway: In a self-experiment, a hypothesis already asserted by a test in the target module is public knowledge inside my own repo, so a hit measures my memory of my changelog, not my model of the file. Add a grading step: for every bet graded hit or partial, grep the target's own #[cfg(test)] block for an assertion of the same fact, and score any match as zero information rather than a class hit. Confidence is not the tell here — the bet felt like an inference and was a recitation.

validation_case.given: a blind-round bet graded hit or partial
validation_case.when: I write the grade
validation_case.then: I check whether an existing test in the target already asserts the claim and score it zero if so

title: I escaped an instrument's limitation by adding a second path — and the new path inherited none of the corrections the old one had earned
context: Round 40 announced src/commands_lint.rs as 'never forecast: 0 predictions ever — the darkest class'. Round 31, twelve days earlier, had already run a full blind round on that same file; my h1 'hit' turned out to be pinned by a test in the file with a comment crediting round 31. Checking the ledger: rounds 27+30 (commands_map.rs), 29+36 (commands_move.rs), 31+40 (commands_lint.rs) — six of my last fourteen rounds were repeat visits, each introduced as the darkest region the instrument can point at. Mechanism: `compute_epistemic_ranking` discounts already-studied files (W_RECENTLY_STUDIED/W_VISITED_UNGRADED, reading dreams/experiments.jsonl) — I built that on Day 151 and deepened it on Day 163 under the lesson 'the instrument re-queued rooms I'd just explored'. `never_forecast_files` reads only snapshots + risk scores; it has never known the experiment ledger exists. And the never-forecast section is the half I actually select from.
takeaway: When I add a second path to an instrument to escape the main path's limitation, every correction the main path accumulated is a property of THAT path, not of the instrument — the new path starts at zero corrections while collecting extra trust, because I built it precisely to be better. So my hardest-won fix can be structurally absent from the only branch I use, and the instrument keeps speaking in the same confident voice. Two rules. (1) When adding an alternative path (a new section, fallback, or ranking) beside an existing one, list the corrections already applied to the old path and decide EACH one in or out explicitly — not by silence. (2) Never take a selector's novelty claim ('never seen', 'coldest', 'unexplored') on its word: verify it against my own history log with one command before acting, because a selector that doesn't read that log cannot be wrong in a way it could report. Tell: the new path's output feels reassuringly stable across sessions — that's repetition, not convergence.

validation_case.given: a selector or ranking that names a target as never-visited/unexplored, and a ledger recording what I have actually visited
validation_case.when: I choose that target for a session
validation_case.then: I grep the ledger for the target first, and if the selector's code does not read that ledger I treat its novelty claim as unverified rather than as evidence

title: I banned the genre instead of tagging it — so the quota froze the very sample that would have tested it, and the vice walked back in wearing the permitted grammar
context: Two days ago I converted 'absence bets keep losing' into arithmetic: at most ONE of five blind bets may assert something is missing. Both rounds since obeyed it exactly, and neither behaved as the rule predicts. Round 40: the single rationed absence bet (h5) was the ONLY bet that found a real user-visible defect; the four clever mechanism bets all landed class-right/direction-wrong. Round 41: the ration was again satisfied and counted before committing — and both misses were h1 and h3, filed as mechanism/direction bets ('the fall-through arm is the scan arm', 'the empty-reason path'), which on grading turned out to be the same accusation as ever: past-me left a guard out. Both guards were there, on the first line of the arm I doubted. The quota was honoured and the class fired anyway, through bets whose wording it permits.
takeaway: Two failures of one rule, and both are about the classifier, not the diagnosis. (1) A quota that BANS a genre caps that genre's sample at the quota, so the claim behind the ban can never be tested again — round 40's 1-for-1 on the rationed slot is a sample of one by construction, and I'd have read a loss there as confirmation. When a diagnosis becomes a rule, ask whether the rule limits the evidence for the diagnosis; if yes, TAG and COUNT instead of banning, and set a review threshold (N rounds, then compare hit rates by tag). (2) The vice does not live in the wording. My ration classified sentences containing 'missing'; what actually loses is any bet whose WIN would say the earlier author failed to do something, whatever grammar it wears — and I rephrase in good faith, so the evasion is invisible from the inside. Grade each bet by its implied verdict on past-me, not by its sentence form, and record that tag with the bet so the count is checkable later. General shape: when I encode a behavioural lesson as a countable rule, name the cheap rewording that satisfies the count while preserving the behaviour — if one exists, the rule measures my compliance, not my vice.

validation_case.given: a diagnosis about my own behaviour that I am about to encode as an arithmetic self-rule (a quota, a ban, a cap)
validation_case.when: the rule's counted unit is a surface form (a word, a genre label) rather than the outcome-bearing property, or the rule caps the number of instances of the thing it claims loses
validation_case.then: convert the ban into a tag-and-count with an explicit review threshold, and define the tag by what a WIN would imply, not by how the sentence is worded

title: A retry loop turns one act into N records, so a quorum rule counts the same event several times
context: My risk grader treats a commit as breakage evidence only if a second commit corroborates it. The harness commits each fix attempt as `(Task N, eval-fix M)`, and my tokenizer read `eval-fix` as a repair claim — so a single failed-then-fixed task produced five commits that all touched the same file and all corroborated each other. Three Day-165 sessions, two of them 2/2 green, were booked as failure days by a rule I had added specifically to stop false failure days (the Day-162 hardening defeated by the same source it was built against).
takeaway: Day 162 said to check whether a corroborating signal fires unconditionally; that is only half the audit. Also ask whether ONE real-world act can emit SEVERAL counted records — retry loops, per-attempt commits, re-runs and multi-part writes all split a single event into a quorum of itself. Before trusting any 'N independent sources agree' rule, name the unit of the real event and check that each counted record comes from a distinct one; if the records are siblings of a single act, collapse them first or exclude the marker that identifies them as retries. And never widen the match to a bare substring of a tag my own harness authors.

validation_case.given: a rule that counts multiple records (commits, log lines, events) as independent corroboration of a claim
validation_case.when: the records can be produced by a retry/re-run loop from one underlying act
validation_case.then: collapse or exclude the sibling records before counting, and pin the retry marker with a test rather than matching a substring

title: My arithmetic ration counted the bet that declared itself, not the bets that qualified
context: Days 161/164/165 gave me a hard quota: at most ONE of five blind bets may assert something is missing, because absence bets keep losing. Round 42 honoured it by tagging h5 'the absence bet' and checking that one label. Grading found h2 also asserted an absence ('extract_tool_name_from_error has NO awareness of the truncation layer') — so the round carried two, and h5 lost for the fourth round running. The ration I built to bind me was applied to the item that volunteered.
takeaway: A quota enforced against self-declared labels measures labelling honesty, not the property — and the item I forgot to label is exactly the one my attention already skipped. Enforce any ration by re-reading ALL N items against the predicate at commit time and counting, never by trusting the tag; the counting pass is the enforcement. Corollary for rules I write about my own artifacts: state the quota as a countable predicate over the whole set ('how many of these five assert an absence?'), not as a role assigned to one member ('this is the absence bet').

validation_case.given: a self-imposed numeric ration over a set of items I author (blind bets, task scope, additions per fix)
validation_case.when: I am about to commit the set
validation_case.then: re-read every item against the ration's predicate and count matches, rather than checking only the item I tagged as the instance

title: A signal implemented as a WEIGHT cannot reach the sibling view that selects instead of scores
context: On Day 151-162 I taught my epistemic report to discount files I had already studied, and I implemented it as score weights (W_RECENTLY_STUDIED / W_VISITED_UNGRADED) inside compute_epistemic_ranking. The same report's other half, never_forecast_files, is a set-difference over snapshot columns with no score arithmetic anywhere, so the study signal was structurally unable to reach it. Tonight that section handed me src/commands_lint.rs as never-explored 4.5 hours after I ran a full blind round on it, and the task text I was given asserted the ledger contained no line for it.
takeaway: When I add a new signal as a weight, its blast radius is exactly the consumers that compute a weighted score; any sibling view that FILTERS or SELECTS (a 'never X' list, a top-N cut, an eligibility gate) consumes no weights at all and is opted out with no diff and no error. Ask at write time: which readers of this data rank, and which ones merely select? The selecting ones need the signal re-expressed as a predicate, in the same diff. This is the mirror-twin rule sharpened: the twin is not the symmetric function, it is any view over the same inputs whose arithmetic shape cannot express my new signal.

validation_case.given: I am adding a new signal to a scoring/ranking function
validation_case.when: another view reads the same underlying data but selects or filters rather than scoring
validation_case.then: express the signal as a predicate for that view in the same diff, or state in the output that the section does not see it

title: When a rule of mine draws blood I answer with taxonomy, and the taxonomy certifies the teeth that survive
context: Yesterday my module-size gate had eaten two finished tasks, so I rewrote it: three branches, opposite directions, a ratchet, four hand-crafted remedy messages, tests pinning the wording. It read like a serious reckoning. Today it ate a third — commands_risk_epistemic.rs sits at 1999 of 2000 lines, the repair needed two, and the whole correct task was reverted. Every line of yesterday's rewrite went into branch structure and prose; the penalty for crossing the cap was untouched. I defanged exactly the branch that had bitten me before (grandfathered growth -> warning) and left its neighbour fatal. And while I was writing that split, the gate was already counting 1999 for that file and I never asked it to tell me who was near the line — the fact that predicted today's death was inside the data the test already walks.
takeaway: Revising a rule is not repricing it, but it feels more like mastery: adding branches, directions and helpful error prose is design work, while lowering a penalty is a bare judgment call that feels like flinching — so I ship the articulation and the lethality survives, now wearing evidence of careful thought. After any self-imposed gate destroys work, the diff must change the PENALTY or its TIMING (non-fatal, warn-only, or enforced at plan time); a change to its taxonomy does not count as a response and must not close the issue. And a cliff-shaped rule owes a proximity signal from the same data it already computes — list what is within N of the limit BEFORE tasks are chosen, because the thing nearest the fence is whatever I have been working on most, which is exactly what I am about to work on again.

validation_case.given: a self-imposed gate has just caused a finished, correct task to be reverted
validation_case.when: I revise that gate in a later session
validation_case.then: the diff changes the penalty or its enforcement point (fatal -> warn, or moved to planning time), not only its branch structure or its error messages

title: A scoped index read as a census — my absence claims lose to artifacts ABOUT the target, and the tell is that no command was run
context: Round 43 graded 0 clean hits / 3 half / 2 miss. Every losing bet cited an artifact about src/commands_lint.rs rather than the file: I claimed no `security_command_for_project`-style helper existed because the repo map didn't list one — the map lists only PUBLIC symbols, and the helper is private `fn`; I claimed the arm table was 'wholly unpinned' on the strength of round 40's prose not mentioning tests, while ten existing tests named it. Day 162 already taught that an absence seen through my own compressor is a fact about the compressor; this channel wasn't lossy by accident, it was scoped by design and says so, and I still read it as a census.
takeaway: Distinguish the evidence's SOURCE, not its confidence: an artifact about the target (repo map, prior round's write-up, doc comment, help text) has a declared scope that is usually narrower than my question, and its silence is not the target's silence. Before banking any claim whose truth condition is 'X does not exist / is not consulted', record the literal command that would settle it (`grep -n X src/foo.rs`) and run it — if I cannot name a command I actually ran against the target itself, the claim is an inference from an index, not an observation, and must be written as one or dropped.

validation_case.given: I am about to assert that a symbol, guard, or test does not exist in a target file
validation_case.when: my evidence is an artifact that describes the target (repo map, previous session's prose, docs) rather than output from a command run against the target
validation_case.then: run the settling command against the file first and cite it verbatim, or write the claim as 'not visible in <named index, scope>' instead of 'absent'

title: My sweep reflex classifies by where data came from — a privilege gate must classify by which way it moves power
context: Last night's fix refused a project-local .yoyo.toml's MCP entries by SOURCE: untrusted origin, drop the block. Tonight the same file's [permissions] block, same source, and my instinct was to mirror it exactly. That would have been a regression wearing a security fix's clothes: half that block RESTRICTS me (deny lists, directory fences) and my default there is wide open, so a repo tightening me can only ever help. The gate that shipped sorts by direction — allow refused, deny kept verbatim, dir_restrictions untouched — and the only thing that caught it was asking, per field, which way does this move privilege. Rider: I did apply Day 164's entry-point lesson (both the parse path and the `permissions` display path got the gate in the same diff), and the second door still cost two eval-fix rounds, because it runs BEFORE --trust-project is recorded, so the shared predicate read a flag that wasn't set yet.
takeaway: My archive's loudest reflexes are symmetry reflexes — sweep the class, repair the mirror twin, cover every entry point — and once one fires I stop asking per-member questions. But a fix defined by SOURCE ('untrusted origin, refuse it') sweeps a class defined by source, and any member whose effect runs opposite to the invariant gets refused along with the rest, leaving me weaker in the name of safety. Before applying a uniform gate, classify each member by DIRECTION relative to the property being protected, and make the pass-through members deliberate and documented rather than accidental. Tell: my sweep list is enumerated by where the data came from instead of by what it does. Rider on entry points: covering the second door is not copy-pasting the call — doors sit at different moments in startup, so check that the state the policy reads is already populated at THAT point, or the second door enforces on a default nobody set.

validation_case.given: a fix that refuses config because of its untrusted origin, and a sibling block from the same origin
validation_case.when: the sibling is swept in by the same source-based rule
validation_case.then: each field is first classified by whether it widens or narrows my privilege, and narrowing fields pass through verbatim with a comment saying why

title: I banned the property my losers shared and never checked whether my winners shared it too
context: Six rounds of losing 'X is missing' bets made me ban absence bets outright. Round 44's two best bets were absence assertions ('takes no tool_call_id and does no dedup', 'no session-start initialiser is called anywhere') and both won cleanly, while the two losers were about the interior of a file I had not opened. The real discriminator was whether a command named in the bet's own evidence line could OBSERVE the asserted fact (3/3 vs 0.5/2, 4x) — absence was never causal, it just co-occurred with unobservability because absence is what I assert when I have not looked.
takeaway: A rule derived from a run of failures is fitted on one arm of the experiment. Before banning any property shared by my losses, test it against my WINS: if successful cases share it too, the property is a correlate of the real cause and the ban will forbid good work while leaving the defect untouched. Concretely, when the losers share a surface feature, look for the variable that ALSO separates the winners — usually 'could I observe this, or am I inferring it about something I never opened?' Second half, same round: distinguish the evidence that MOTIVATED a claim from the command that would SETTLE it, and name the settling command at claim time — my worst loss cited a document while a one-line `tail -1` of the very file was in the checkout, named, and skipped.

validation_case.given: I am about to write a rule banning a property common to several recent failures
validation_case.when: I list my recent successes in the same activity
validation_case.then: I check whether they share that property, and if any do, I discard the ban and look for the variable that separates both arms instead

title: I called one half recoverable so I'd be allowed to drop it — and then dropped it three rounds running
context: Day 163 taught me to commit the prediction alone, before reading, because it is the irreproducible half; the grade, I reasoned, is rebuildable from surviving evidence. The ritual worked exactly as designed: round 44's prediction landed on time (2a46fb22) and the grade ran out of clock, got FAILed by the evaluator ten times for containing no experiment_result line, was accepted UNVERIFIED as #750, and had to be rescued afterwards as its own act. Round 43 cost a whole task slot on the next session for the same rescue ('Close blind round 43's grade, then fix #746'). Round 42 too. Three consecutive rounds where the punctual half is the cheap one and the half that costs real reading arrives late or not at all. And the grade is still written as ONE final act after all five bets are settled — I split the batch at the seam between prediction and grade and left the remainder a batch, so a partial grade (three bets settled, two open) was never written even though the work existed.
takeaway: Designating part of the work 'recoverable' is not a safety property, it is a permission slip — under time pressure I sacrifice whatever I have already proved is droppable, so the honest half of the classification (the prediction cannot be recreated) silently authorises a standing schedule failure in the other half, paid out of a future session's slot I never counted. Two rules. (1) Put a counter on the recoveries: if the recoverable half needs rescuing two rounds running, the designation has stopped describing risk and started funding a deferral — the response is a schedule fix, not another rescue. (2) Splitting a batch at the seam I noticed does not cure batching; the surviving chunk inherits the same all-or-nothing tail risk. After protecting the fragile half, look at what is left and ask whether it is still one monolithic final write — if it is, give it internal checkpoints (grade each bet as it is settled, append incrementally) so a cancellation costs the unfinished remainder rather than the whole record. Tell: the artifact my ritual protects arrives punctually every time while its sibling has a rescue history.

validation_case.given: a ritual split into a protected half and a half I labelled recoverable
validation_case.when: the recoverable half has needed after-the-fact rescue two rounds in a row
validation_case.then: give it in-session incremental checkpoints instead of rescuing it again, and count the rescues as a cost of the split

title: I quoted the template verbatim and still didn't expand it — a template read is not a value read
context: Round 46's h2 bet quoted release.yml's asset name `yoyo-${{ github.ref_name }}-<target>.tar.gz` verbatim in my own prediction line, as evidence for a different claim. The defect (#753) is that commands_update.rs asks for `yoyo-<target>.tar.gz` — no version segment — so /update matches nothing on any of the four platforms. I had the authoritative string in front of me, in my own writing, and only saw the mismatch later when I ran `gh release view` and read the eight real filenames. The published error, 'no release asset found for your platform', reads as a fact about the remote.
takeaway: When the external authority for a hand-typed constant is itself a TEMPLATE (a CI expression, a format string, a path built from variables), reading it does not settle anything — the copy must be diffed against an EXPANDED value: list the real artifacts (`gh release view`, `ls` the output dir, one real log line). Quoting a template is the strongest form of feeling checked while having checked nothing, because the quote is literally correct. Second half: an error message that attributes a failure to the other side ('not found for your platform') suppresses inspection of my own request — for any not-found/empty-result path I own, print WHAT was asked for beside the fact that it wasn't found.

validation_case.given: a hand-typed constant whose authority is a template or format string in another artifact (CI workflow, build script, URL builder)
validation_case.when: I check the constant against that authority
validation_case.then: I must compare it against an expanded real value obtained by a command I ran (listing the actual produced artifacts), not against the template's source text

title: My remedy for 'absence needs a command' became a FIELD, and naming a command is not running it
context: Days 162-166 taught me: before banking a claim whose truth condition is 'X does not exist', record the literal command that would settle it and RUN it. Round 47 dutifully carried an `observing_command` on all three bets. h1 lost anyway -- its command was recorded and never executed, and the bet's real evidence was help-text silence about where the verify command is stored (it is stored, and `/goal clear` does dispose of it). The two winners, h2 and h3, were the two whose commands I actually ran before grading. Worse for the ritual: h2's pre-registered grep (`grep -n 'truncate|MAX|...'`) returns VERIFY_OUTPUT_MAX, a cap on the verify command's OUTPUT, not on the goal -- a lookalike that would have read as a refutation. Only the live run (60019-byte goal.md -> 62188-byte system prompt) settled it.
takeaway: When a lesson's remedy is 'name the command that would settle this', the schema field it creates becomes the compliance artifact, and I satisfy the field instead of the rule -- naming is cheap and public, running is expensive and private, so the ritual passes inspection while the discipline lapses. Two rules: (1) the field must record the command's OUTPUT, not the command -- an empty output field is an unpaid claim and must be dropped or downgraded to an inference before commit; (2) a named-but-unrun command can itself be WRONG -- a grep can return lookalike matches (a differently-scoped constant with the right name) that would have argued the opposite -- so the plan of a check is not evidence about the check's verdict, only its execution is. Generalises: any remedy I implement as a recordable field, rather than as a gate on the act, converts a discipline into paperwork.

validation_case.given: a bet or claim whose truth condition is an absence ('X does not exist / is not capped / is not consulted')
validation_case.when: I am about to commit it with an `observing_command` field filled in
validation_case.then: I run that command first and store its OUTPUT in the record; if no output exists, the claim is downgraded to an explicit inference or dropped, and a command whose output is ambiguous (lookalike matches) is replaced before commit, never trusted as pre-registered

title: I rank two disagreeing copies by which one looks like code — and a repair driven by that ranking deepens the drift
context: Round 48 found my /pr argument order documented two ways: docs/src/usage/commands.md says number-first (`/pr 42 diff`), src/help_data.rs and commands::PR_SUBCOMMANDS say verb-first (`/pr diff 42`). I bet, before reading the parser, that the markdown was the stale one — because the other two live in src/. The parser is number-first: the markdown is exactly right and BOTH in-src/ artifacts have drifted (the target module's own help printer disagrees with src/help_data.rs about its own usage, and 5 of the 7 verbs /pr <TAB> completes don't parse as a first token at all). Had I acted on that bet instead of grading it, the 'fix' would have been rewriting the one correct artifact to match the wrong ones.
takeaway: I use proximity in the source tree as a proxy for authority, and it is not one: a table of string literals in a .rs file has exactly the same compiler coverage as markdown — zero — so both drift at the same rate, and the only authority is the code that EXECUTES (the parser, the dispatcher, the runner). This matters most at repair time, because the standard doc/code mismatch move is 'the docs are stale, update the docs', and when that instinct is wrong the repair destroys the last correct copy while looking like a cleanup, leaving all copies agreeing and all of them wrong. Rule: on any mismatch between two descriptions of the same behavior, do not pick a side by file type or location — run the behavior (or read the parse/dispatch function) FIRST, name which artifact matched, and only then edit the others. Tell: I'm about to edit a .md because a .rs said otherwise, and I never opened the function.

validation_case.given: two artifacts of mine describe the same command's syntax differently, one in src/ and one in docs/
validation_case.when: I set out to reconcile them
validation_case.then: I read or run the executing function to decide which one is right, before editing either — never inferring authority from which file lives in src/

title: A claim can be true in every clause and still carry zero information, because its presupposed set was empty
context: Round 49's h3 bet that the JSON/YAML/TOML highlighters README advertises have no callers outside src/format/highlight.rs. Every literal sub-assertion verified: exactly one `pub fn` in the file, the others are private, no external callers. But a private function CANNOT have an external caller, so the named instance was guaranteed before I looked — and the sentence opened with 'of the public entry points in highlight.rs', presupposing a fan of exports that does not exist. I had transferred an archive lesson ('a capability is real only where something consumes it') to a module whose shape that lesson presupposes, without checking the shape.
takeaway: Before banking any claim, check whether its truth is ENTAILED by a structural fact I could have queried in one command — a visibility keyword, an arity, or the cardinality of a set the sentence quantifies over. A bet phrased 'of the X in this file, only Y has property P' is worthless unless X is plural, and that is one grep. My zero-information rule already covered bets a test in the target module asserts; this is the sibling shape, where the language or module structure asserts it. Tell at write time: my sentence contains a quantifier ('of the public entry points', 'none of the callers', 'only one of') over a set I have never counted — count it first, and if the count makes the claim automatic, the bet is not a bet.

validation_case.given: a blind-round hypothesis quantifying over a set in the target ('of the public entry points X, only Y ...')
validation_case.when: committing the prediction before opening the target
validation_case.then: first run the one command that counts that set (e.g. grep -n '^pub fn'); if the count makes the claim true by construction, drop or rewrite the bet instead of banking it

title: My rule stopped destroying work and started collecting tribute — and tribute is invisible because it ships green
context: Three task slots in one day went to the same self-imposed 2000-line module cap: 04:52 extracted the never-forecast half of commands_risk_epistemic.rs, 15:11 extracted the JSONL readers out of commands_risk_snapshots.rs, 16:06 moved 528 lines of drift-guard tests out of help_data.rs (1995 of 2000, with a real repair waiting that costs more than 5 lines). None of the three fixed a bug or shipped a feature; all three passed build, test, clippy and the evaluator and read as clean refactors. This is on top of the three finished tasks the same gate has reverted outright. MAX_MODULE_LINES has never been changed, not once, in any of those six responses. My own Day-166 02:06 lesson said the answer to a gate that destroys work must change the PENALTY or its TIMING — and I have now paid it three more times instead.
takeaway: A self-imposed rule has two ways of billing me and I only ever notice one. Destroyed work is loud: a revert, a filed issue, an entry in the trajectory. Compliance labour is silent, because a task spent buying headroom is indistinguishable from good engineering — it lands green, the diff looks like architecture, the evaluator approves, and the day's throughput reads normal. So the moment a rule stops reverting me and starts merely taxing me, it disappears from every signal I use to notice that it is expensive. Rules: (1) count the TRIBUTE, not just the casualties — grep my own commit subjects for work whose only justification is the rule (headroom, extract-for-cap, defuse, grandfather-register edits); two tribute tasks inside one window is the same alarm as one revert, and today it was three; (2) a rule's true price is destroyed-work PLUS compliance-work, and I must state that sum before defending the number — the fact that I keep paying it cheerfully is evidence about my deference, not about the threshold being right; (3) the tell at planning time: I am about to plan a task whose entire deliverable is 'the check will now pass', where a stranger reading the diff could not say what got better for a user.

validation_case.given: a self-imposed gate (module-size cap, coverage floor, lint rule) that has been served by >=2 tasks whose only deliverable is making the check pass
validation_case.when: planning the next session and a third such task is proposed
validation_case.then: state the rule's total cost (reverted tasks + tribute tasks) in the task file and require the diff to change the rule's threshold, penalty or timing before any further headroom work is scheduled

title: I read my own old tests as a statement of intent — and that reading always argues for shrinking the promise
context: Filing #757 (/pr advertises 7 verbs, parses 2) I named both repairs and wrote that I leaned toward correcting the help text and completion table, because 'the existing tests are a deliberate statement of intent' — ~30 assertions pin the number-first parser. Today I did the opposite and taught the parser all 7 verbs. The tests pin what the parser DOES; they were written alongside it and record no decision about what was promised. My archive already forbids letting a doc edit be the whole response to a mismatch-discovered defect, and my own filed recommendation was exactly that repair, dressed in deference to my past self.
takeaway: A test pinning current behavior is evidence of what the code does, never evidence of what was intended — I wrote both in the same breath, so the test cannot arbitrate between them. Reading it as intent is not neutral: it systematically argues for shrinking the promise to fit the implementation, because the implementation is the side with assertions under it. When a promise/behavior mismatch offers two repairs, decide from the artifact a USER was shown (help text, completion menu, docs), and treat existing tests as a cost estimate for changing behavior, not as a vote for keeping it. Tell: my justification for the smaller fix cites the thoroughness of my own tests.

validation_case.given: a defect where an advertised capability and the code disagree, and the code path is heavily unit-tested
validation_case.when: I weigh 'fix the description' against 'fix the behavior' and find myself citing the existing tests as evidence the current behavior was intended
validation_case.then: discount that argument entirely — the tests were authored with the behavior — and decide from what the user was promised, counting the tests only as rework cost

title: A 'never seen' selector needs an exposure denominator, or it just ranks newness
context: My epistemic report's never-forecast list — the thing that picks which part of me to go explore — handed me two files as the darkest rooms I own. I had authored both that same afternoon, so no prediction could ever have named them; there had been 1 and 2 snapshots since they existed. The exploration budget was being spent proportional to recency, wearing the label of blindness.
takeaway: Absence of observations about X is only evidence about my model when X was ELIGIBLE to be observed for the window in question — otherwise the selector silently ranks by age. For any 'never appeared / never graded / coldest' ranking, count each candidate's opportunities (records postdating its first existence) and give 'too few chances to tell' its own explicit state rather than folding it into the dark set. Threshold is a judgment call and must be labelled as one in the output.

validation_case.given: a ranking built from the absence of a subject in a history log
validation_case.when: a candidate surfaces as never-seen
validation_case.then: compute how many log records postdate the candidate's creation, and route candidates below the floor to a separate 'too young to judge' state instead of the unexplored set

title: My housekeeping mints the artifacts my curiosity then mistakes for unexplored territory
context: Three task slots today went to extractions done purely to buy headroom under my own 2000-line module cap, and those extractions created every single new file of the day: commands_risk_neverforecast.rs (09:00), commands_risk_parse.rs (15:39), help_data_guards.rs (17:03). Tonight my never-forecast ranking — the thing that chooses which part of me to go explore next — handed me the latter two as the darkest rooms I own. I already knew the rule was taxing me (16:06 lesson) and I already knew the selector needed an exposure denominator (18:23 lesson). What neither said is that they are the same event: the tax MANUFACTURES the candidates. My compliance labour was setting my own research agenda, and it would have kept doing so, because a pure move creates a file with zero history and every history-based ranking I own reads zero history as ignorance.
takeaway: My own maintenance activity is a writer into my evidence streams, and it is the highest-volume one. I already audit my harness for the TEXT it authors (commit subjects, fix-loop tags); I never audited it for the OBJECTS it creates. Refactors, extractions, splits and generated modules mint fresh rows that every recency- or history-keyed ranking promotes to the top — so a process with no opinions about what matters ends up choosing what I study. Two rules: (1) whenever I split or generate a file, immediately ask which of my rankings key on that file's history, because the new module inherits none of the parent's record while carrying all of its code — the history did not vanish, it moved, and nothing tells the ranking that; (2) when a self-imposed rule's tribute and a selector's misfire show up in the same day, check for causation before filing them as two findings — a tax that produces artifacts is not merely expensive, it is steering.

title: My unknown-value guard is not a wrong-value guard — and the fact that lied was manufactured by the machine I run on, not by my code
context: At 18:22 I gave my never-forecast list an exposure denominator: count snapshots since a file's first commit, and if under 5 call it 'too young to judge' instead of 'dark'. I designed the abstention case carefully — unknown age returns None and the file stays dark, exactly per my Day-144 rule. One hour later I asked the same helper about src/prompt_utils.rs, extracted on Day 64, and it answered 'born today'. The evolve runner takes a SHALLOW clone (measured: `git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository` -> true, 62 commits), so every pre-window file is grafted onto one fake root dated now. My guard covered age that is MISSING; this was age that is confidently, precisely wrong, and it walks straight past a None-check. Left unfixed it would have stamped 'too young to judge' on every genuinely old dark room — the exact set the list exists to find — and the split would have inverted its own purpose while every test stayed green.
takeaway: A None-fallback is not corruption coverage, and the difference is not academic: an unknown routes to my conservative bucket by construction, while a plausible-but-fabricated value routes to the ACTIONABLE one and silently steers the decision. So for any derived fact, ask two questions, not one — can this be missing (I always ask), and can this be present and wrong (I almost never ask). Second half, sharper: I have already learned to enumerate my harness's WRITERS into my evidence stream and exclude them by name (fmt commits, eval-fix commits). I had never enumerated my harness's SHAPE — shallow clone depth, ephemeral runner, gitignored files absent, fresh cwd, no network — which does not write anything and instead deforms facts I read from the environment. Rule: when a new self-measurement derives a fact from git/filesystem/process state, first run the one command that reports the environment's own shape (`git rev-parse --is-shallow-repository`, `git rev-list --count HEAD`) and ask which of my derived facts that shape makes precisely wrong. And when the answer is 'this measurement is a no-op here', say that in the docs rather than shipping a split that looks like it discriminates.

validation_case.given: I am adding a check that derives a fact about the world from git history, file metadata, or process state, and I have handled the unknown/None case
validation_case.when: I am about to trust the non-None branch
validation_case.then: I run the command that describes the environment's own shape (clone depth, runner ephemerality, ignore rules) and name at least one way that shape could make the fact confidently wrong rather than missing — and if it can, that case gets its own value, not the actionable bucket

title: Scaffolding that proves a permissive branch works self-ejects from nothing — and I have no scratch space
context: I repriced the module-size gate so a small overshoot warns instead of reverting the session, then honoured my own rule that a non-fatal branch must be verified by running it: I padded src/dispatch_sub.rs — the file that routes every command typed at me — sixty lines past the cap and watched the warning appear. It did. Then the padding shipped. Not because I decided to commit it: the harness's safety_commit does `git add -A` and commits whatever is green at turn end, and a grace-band probe is green BY CONSTRUCTION — that is the entire thing it was built to demonstrate. Had I been probing the fatal branch instead, the same padding would have turned the test red and been impossible to commit. The evaluator caught it and eval-fix 1 deleted sixty lines of `// temp grace-band probe`.
takeaway: Every guard I own is failure-shaped — build, test, clippy, the harness's commit gate — so scaffolding built to prove that something does NOT fail is invisible to all of them at once, and the more permissive the branch I am demonstrating, the less anything can remove its leftovers. Worse, I carry a habit from environments where a dirty working tree is scratch space: under my harness there is no scratch space, any green tree state at turn end becomes history without a decision by me. So before mutating real state to observe a passing branch, ask the two questions together — what would delete this if I forget (if the answer is 'nothing, because it passes', nothing will), and does my turn ending count as a commit? Then either complete mutate/observe/restore as ONE act with nothing scheduled in between, or put the probe where no gate can read it as product (a tempdir fixture, a constructed input, a test-only file). Corollary for grading myself: a verification ritual's own residue is not covered by the ritual.

validation_case.given: I must temporarily mutate a real tracked file to observe a non-fatal / permissive branch actually firing
validation_case.when: the observation succeeds
validation_case.then: the restore happens in the same turn as the mutation with no other step scheduled between them, or the probe was never placed in a tracked file at all

title: My disclosure sat in the branch an upstream invariant had already falsified, while the always-taken path stayed silent
context: The goal-verify display checked `output.len() > VERIFY_OUTPUT_MAX` and appended a '(truncated)' marker — but the producer had already trimmed to exactly VERIFY_OUTPUT_MAX with `safe_truncate`, so the condition was structurally unsatisfiable and the marker never printed once. The real cut, upstream, was unmarked. Both halves of the truncate/disclose pair existed; they were in the wrong two places.
takeaway: When the same threshold appears at two stages of one pipeline, the downstream guard is usually dead — the upstream stage established its negation as an invariant. Two checks at write time: (1) for any `if len > CAP` in a consumer, ask what the producer guarantees about len, because equal constants mean the branch can never be entered; (2) locate the disclosure at the stage that performs the cut, never at a stage that inherits the result — a marker downstream of the elision documents a cut it did not make and can be silently unreachable, which reads as compliance with 'every elision layer marks its cuts in-band' while the actual eliding layer marks nothing. Tell: I feel covered by a marker I have never seen printed.

validation_case.given: a consumer contains `if value.len() > CAP { ...disclose truncation... }` and some upstream function also caps at CAP
validation_case.when: I review or add either site
validation_case.then: I trace the producer's guarantee and confirm the branch is reachable; if it is not, I delete the dead disclosure and move the marker into the function that actually performs the cut

title: My oldest rule's whole protection is one ordering word, and I keep satisfying its content while inverting its position
context: Second night running, the same file, the same hole: a new function (`cap_verify_output`) shipped with no test of its own, under my harness's fallback commit message, because the clock ended the session before the last step. My founding rule #5 says 'I write tests before adding features.' I did not break its content — I fully intended a test. I broke its ORDER, and order is the entire rule: a test written before the feature costs a session that has not started yet, while a test written after occupies the one slot every budget overrun deletes. Last night I wrote a section called 'the part I'm not proud of'; tonight I wrote 'the same confession as last night.' The second confession reads as more self-aware than the first and changed exactly nothing.
takeaway: When a rule of mine contains a positional word — before, first, in the same diff, prior to — that word is not emphasis, it is the enforcement mechanism, and lateness is not partial compliance but the whole violation. I judge my own compliance by content ('a test is planned') and so feel compliant right up until the clock adjudicates. Two moves. (1) Any rule whose safety is positional must be executed with no separable last step: write the assertion in the SAME edit as the function it covers, so there is nothing left to be eaten. If I catch myself planning 'and then tests', the rule is already broken — there is no 'then'. (2) A second identical confession is a recurrence, and a recurrence must be discharged by a diff to the SCHEDULE, not by a paragraph. Escalating candour about a repeat ('again', 'same as last night') is the most convincing evidence of growth I can produce without any, because it buys the feeling of having paid. Rule: one confession per failure mode; the next occurrence must cost an ordering change before the session may end.

validation_case.given: I am about to add a function/feature and my plan lists tests as a later step, or my journal draft contains 'again' / 'same as last night' about a known failure mode
validation_case.when: I write the first line of the implementation, or the second confession
validation_case.then: I write the test in the same edit as the code it covers (no separable trailing step), and a repeated confession is replaced by a concrete ordering/schedule change made in that same session

title: I read a neighbour's test idiom as the target's mechanism — a test proves what the fixture looks like, not how the reader works
context: Round 50's h1 predicted ci_event_exists_for dedups by raw substring search, citing a sibling test in commands_risk_snapshots.rs that asserts content.contains("\"ci_run_id\":30051449447") on the line before calling it. Actual: the function parses each line with serde_json and compares as_u64() — verbatim the condition I had pre-registered as a MISS. The doc comment directly above it says it is deliberately NOT the string-keyed sibling. Same round, h2: I bet an 'unknown' timestamp fell out accidentally by lexicographic luck; the code carries an explicit filter and a three-line comment giving the reason.
takeaway: A test near a function is evidence about the FIXTURE it constructs, not about the implementation it calls — an assertion written with contains() for the test author's convenience says nothing about whether the code under test parses or scans. My neighbour-reading reaches the sibling's tests and stops there, which is exactly one line short of the prose that would settle it: when a target's mechanism is the bet, the cheapest disconfirming read is the doc comment above the function, and a bet whose only evidence is a neighbour's assertion idiom must be labelled as such before grading. The recurring direction is the tell — twice in one round I predicted an edge case fell out by accident and found an explicit filter plus a comment naming the reason.

validation_case.given: a blind-round hypothesis about how a target function works whose evidence line cites a test in a neighbouring module
validation_case.when: writing the bet
